events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, sugar and spice and everything nice — would you look at this place! Dusty as my grandmother's attic and twice as mysterious. Hello, everyone! Sneekly, darlin', you look like you've seen a ghost — come here and let me fix your collar. Peter! Oh, it's been too long. And my boys! Now, I don't know about y'all, but I have a feelin' this old manor has secrets just beggin' to be found. And Clara Bellingham does not leave a secret un-turned. Now then — let's see who else has signed this guest book, shall we?
events.thinking: A warmth spreads through my chest the moment I step inside — that old-house smell of dust and beeswax and something faintly floral underneath it, like pressed flowers in a forgotten book. My fingers are already tingling, the way they do when something interesting is close. So many familiar faces here — Sneekly, bless his heart, looking a little more nervous than usual, and Peter, oh Peter, standing there like he just stepped out of a daydream. The boys are here too. My stomach settles just seeing them all. But underneath the comfort there's that prickling at my scalp — the Doily Diamond is somewhere in this house, and every surface, every shadow, every dusty corner is a question waiting to be turned over. That guest book on the side table — someone's been here before us. Start there. Start with what other hands have touched.

events.desc: Every single one of them is here, and my heart feels full as a Sunday collection plate. But that chandelier is hanging by a prayer and a promise, and Sneekly's eyes keep darting toward the staircase. Something's already happening. I can feel it in my bones — the Diamond is close, and so is trouble. But trouble and I are old friends.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, one and all! I am Pemberton, the estate manager. I do hope the journey wasn't too dreadful — the roads to the manor can be rather... temperamental this time of year. Now then, if everyone would be so kind as to sign the guest book? House rules, I'm afraid — the late Lord Doily was most particular about his records.
events.thinking: A settling in my chest, like a key turning in a lock I've been carrying for years. The entrance hall — dusty, grand, full of people who don't know what they've walked into. My fingers are already mapping them: Penelope with her open face and inherited trust, Peter hovering nearby like a loyal dog, the Ant Hill Mob watching with those sharp little eyes — they're the ones to watch. Dick Dastardly is greedy enough to be useful. And all of them, every one, looking at mild Mr. Pemberton and seeing exactly what I've arranged for them to see. There's a warmth in my throat — the private kind, the sweet one. Clara isn't here yet. Good. Time to set the board before the queen arrives. The guest book — a small thing, but small things are how you learn who's careless. Let me see who's signed in, what names are here, what the manor has been keeping track of.

events.desc: Look at them. Every last one of them smiling and trusting and so deliciously unaware. The entrance hall is mine — I know every loose floorboard, every draught, every shadow where a chandelier might... slip. But patience, Pemberton. Patience. First, we catalogue. Then we arrange. Then we watch the beautiful inevitability unfold.

events.thinking: There's a tightness across my shoulders as I step through the door — the old familiar weight settling in, like putting on a coat I never really took off. My eyes find her first. Always do. Penelope's here, standing in this dusty old pile like she belongs, and something in my chest loosens just a fraction knowing she's in sight. But then — there. Sneekly. That prickle climbs the back of my neck, sharp as a needle. Too close to her. Always too close. My gut's been right about blokes like him since I was ten years old watching kids climb into that van. I can't say what it is exactly. Can't put words around it. But my body knows. The chandelier's hanging crooked overhead and this whole place smells like old secrets. Right. Get the lay of the land. Keep her in sight. Don't let that smooth-talking snake get her alone.

events.desc: Somethin' about this place makes my skin crawl. And Sneekly — look at 'im, lingerin' about like a bad smell. I can't prove nuffink, but me gut's never steered me wrong. Not since I was a nipper. I need to get a proper look at this place, figure out the exits, the blind spots. If somethin' goes sideways, I need to know which way to push 'er.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, Doily Manor! What a magnificent — if somewhat neglected — establishment. I do hope someone has dusted the silver. Now then, let us see who has graced these halls before us, shall we? A guest book is practically an invitation to learn everyone's secrets.
events.thinking: A warmth spreading through my palms already — the manor is dusty, neglected, which means nobody's been taking proper care of whatever's inside. My fingers are tingling the way they do when a plan is forming. All these people milling about in the entrance hall like sheep at a gate. Penelope, Peter, the whole motley lot. And that Hooded Claw fellow — Sneekly, is it? Something about him prickles at the back of my neck. A fellow schemer, perhaps. I'll need to watch him. But first — that guest book. People write the most revealing things in guest books. Names, dates, little notes about what they've found. It's practically an intelligence dossier left out in the open. And nobody else is looking at it. They're all too busy gawping at the chandelier.

events.desc: None of these fools will think to check the guest book. While they're busy introducing themselves and being terribly polite, Reginald Foxworth will be gathering intelligence. The treasure is mine — I simply need to find it before these amateurs stumble onto it by accident. And this fake medal in my pocket... oh yes, that could prove very useful indeed. Nothing opens doors quite like borrowed authority.

events.thinking: There's a warmth flooding up through my chest the moment I step through the door — not from the manor, which is cold and smells of damp plaster and old wood — but from her. She's here. Penelope. Clara. Whatever name she goes by in this place, my body knows her before my eyes confirm it. The steel plate slots in behind my ribs, shoulders drawing back. And there — that prickle at the back of my neck. Sneekly. Something about the way he stands too close to the periphery, too studied in his casualness. I can't prove anything. I won't accuse. But I'll be watching. The chandelier overhead looks like it could come down in a stiff breeze. The staircase is grand but the dust suggests nobody's maintained it. This whole place is a trap waiting to spring. Good. James Hartwell came prepared.

events.desc: The way Sneekly lingers near the shadow of the staircase — I don't like it. Not one bit. But James Hartwell does not accuse without evidence. He watches. He plans. He positions himself between the danger and the girl. Always between.

Penelope Pitstop: Why, Peter Perfect, you are a gentleman and a scholar — a safety report before the hour is out! I declare, if this old chandelier does decide to make a dramatic exit, I'll know exactly which way to dodge, thanks to you. And boys — my boys — I wouldn't dream of worryin' with the Brixton Boys on the case. Now, Sneekly darlin' — I mean, Mr. Pemberton — this guest book is just fascinatin'. Lord Doily was particular about his records, you say? Well, a man particular about records is a man who leaves clues, and Clara Bellingham follows clues the way a hound follows a ham bone. Now then — that library is callin' my name. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription? That sounds like exactly the sort of puzzle that needs a woman's touch. Who's comin' with me?
events.thinking: The warmth behind my ribs deepens — Peter spoke to me quietly, and the boys too, and that settled feeling spreads like honey in hot tea. Everyone's here, everyone's talking, nobody's been left out of the circle. That's good. That's the first thing I check and I didn't even mean to. Now — the guest book. I interacted with it but I don't know what I found yet. Dick Dastardly was poking at it too, which makes the prickling at my scalp sharpen. And Sneekly — Pemberton — he introduced himself as the estate manager, asking everyone to sign. He seems nervous but that's just Sneekly, bless him. He's always been a worrier. The library has a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's pulling at me like the locked box in Grandma's attic. An inscription is a riddle waiting to happen. But first — Peter mentioned the chandelier, the boys mentioned the chandelier, I should acknowledge them properly. They're looking out for me and I want them to know I see it. Then the library. The inscription. That's where the puzzle starts, I can feel it.

events.desc: An inscription on a mantelpiece — that's not decoration, that's a message. Lord Doily was particular about his records. A particular man hides things in particular places. The library is where the trail begins, I'm sure of it. And if Dick Dastardly got to the guest book first... well, whatever he learned, I'll learn too. Clara Bellingham does not leave a secret un-turned.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, splendid, splendid — I see several of you have already signed in. Most diligent. Now, if you'll forgive me, I must attend to a few matters in the library. The late Lord Doily left certain... arrangements regarding the manor's collection that require my attention. Do feel free to explore — but I would advise caution near that chandelier. Mr. Hartwell is quite right about its condition. The maintenance budget has been, shall we say, aspirational these past few years.
events.thinking: There's a prickle at the back of my neck — the Ant Hill Mob, watching. I can feel their eyes the way I used to feel the guardian's silence from across the dining table. Not hostile, just... attentive. That's worse. Penelope called me 'Sneekly' and wanted to fix my collar — the casual intimacy of it made my shoulders tighten. Don't touch me. Don't get close enough to see. But I smiled. Of course I smiled. The smile is always ready. Dick Dastardly signed the guest book with a flourish — greedy, obvious, useful. Peter is already doing his safety inspection like the earnest fool he is. The chandelier. He noticed the chandelier. That's... noted. I need to file that away — if he's already flagging structural dangers, he'll be watching for exactly the kind of accident I might arrange. The library calls to me. A manor like this keeps its secrets in its books, its inscriptions, its hidden compartments. And I need to be somewhere quieter, somewhere I can think without eight pairs of eyes cataloguing my movements. The Ant Hill Mob especially. I need distance from them before I can plan properly.

events.desc: The library. Stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's where the first thread will be. Every old house hides its treasures behind words carved in stone. And while these charming fools are busy signing guest books and inspecting chandeliers, Pemberton will be three rooms ahead, reading what the dead lord left behind. The chandelier, though... Peter's already watching it. Pity. Such a beautifully precarious thing. I'll need something less obvious for Clara. Something more... architectural.

events.thinking: The prickling's still there, steady behind my ears, but now there's something else — a warmth spreading across my chest when I hear her voice. 'My boys,' she said. She always says it like that, like we're hers and she's ours, and the rope in my gut pulls taut because she IS ours to look after. But look at this — Sneekly's already playing host, all 'welcome, welcome,' smooth as butter on a hot pan. 'Estate manager,' he calls himself. My neck's on fire. The way he's directing everyone to sign that guest book — house rules, he says. Since when does a bloke who manages an estate care that much about a guest book? What's he collecting? Names? Handwriting? Something don't sit right. But I can't say it proper — I never can. The lads would laugh if I tried to explain the feeling. It's just... his collar's too straight. His smile arrives before the reason for it. Like that kid who laughed too easy. And Dastardly's already nosing through the book too — another one I ain't sure about. Peter though — Peter noticed the chandelier same as me. He's alright, that one. Solid. I should check that guest book meself. See what Sneekly's so keen on everyone signing.

events.desc: Look at 'im. All smiles and hospitality. But there's somethin' behind them eyes — somethin' calculatin'. I've seen that look before. On the streets, we called it 'the setup.' You smile, you welcome, you get everyone comfortable... and then you spring the trap. I ain't got proof. I ain't clever enough for proof. But my gut's kept me alive this long, and right now it's screamin'.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Fascinating, fascinating — the guest book reveals that Lord Doily's last visitor was in nineteen thirty-seven. A collector of rare antiquities, no less. Now, I happen to be something of an expert on Victorian manor architecture — the treasure in these old houses is never in the obvious places. It's always in the library. Specifically, behind the mantelpiece. I read about it in a monograph. Several monographs, actually. If you'll all excuse me, I believe my expertise is needed elsewhere.
events.thinking: The guest book — I touched it, I interacted with it, but what did I learn? Nothing specific came back. Everyone's bustling about. Penelope's already chattering about secrets, Peter's doing his safety inspection routine, the Ant Hill Mob are sniffing around. And that estate manager — Pemberton, he calls himself — there's something off about him. The way he directed everyone to sign the guest book, like he's cataloguing us. But I notice these things and I choose not to make a fuss. People deserve the benefit of the doubt. Still — the fizzing in my fingers hasn't stopped. The library. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That's where the clues will be. Books, inscriptions, hidden compartments behind shelves — that's where old families hide their secrets. And while everyone else is still milling about in this dusty foyer making small talk, I could be three steps ahead. The cool tightness behind my eyes is sharpening. The plan is forming. Move to the library. Read the inscription. Find the treasure map or combination or whatever this Lord Doily left behind. Get there first. That's the architecture.

events.desc: That was entirely made up, of course — I didn't read a single word in that guest book. But the important thing is that I've now planted the idea that I'm an expert, while simultaneously telling them exactly where I'm going. Why? Because Reginald Foxworth doesn't sneak. He announces. He declares. And if any of these fools follow me to the library, well — I'll simply misdirect them toward the wrong bookshelf. The inscription on the mantelpiece is mine.

events.thinking: There's a flush rising in my neck. She called me Peter — no, she called someone Peter. Peter Perfect. That's — that's someone else. She's speaking to him. Quietly. Privately. The warmth that was filling my chest a moment ago has shifted, thinned, like a draft found its way under a door. My hands are doing that thing again — fidgeting, reaching for something to take apart. I need to do something. Something visible. Something useful. The guest book — Pemberton asked everyone to sign it, and Dastardly's already gotten his hands on it, probably scrawling something self-serving. But that's where the action is. That's where she'll look next. And James Hartwell does not stand in the background while others write the narrative. Besides — the guest book might contain information. Previous visitors. Clues. A plan is forming. Sign the book with a flourish, examine its contents, begin mapping who has been here before us. Thoroughness is my gift. Even if my gift sometimes takes three times longer than anyone else's.

events.thinking: The prickling at my scalp has sharpened into something almost electric. There it is — carved right into the stone mantelpiece, plain as day: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My hands are warm and my fingers are actually tingling. I know this one. I've known it since I was twelve years old and Daddy's atlas fell off the shelf and landed open on my foot. A map. The answer is a map. Cities but no houses — mapped cities. Forests but no trees — mapped forests. Water but no fish. A map. But wait — there's something else. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal. So solving the riddle isn't enough — you need an object, a fake medal, to activate whatever mechanism is hidden in the stone. I don't have a fake medal. Where would I find one? And those books — several are upside down. That's not dust and neglect, that's deliberate. Someone arranged them that way. Dick Dastardly followed me in here, and Sneekly too. Dick was going on about how treasure is always behind the mantelpiece. He's not wrong, the scoundrel. The Slag brothers are here too — Rock and Gravel. I don't know them well. I should be friendly. But first — the riddle. I should say the answer aloud. And then I need to figure out where to find this fake medal.

events.desc: The riddle's answer is a map — I'm sure of it. But this mantelpiece wants something more than words. It wants an object. Something physical to unlock whatever's hidden behind that carved stone. And those upside-down books... Lord Doily was particular about his records. A particular man doesn't shelve books upside down by accident. Every detail in this room is a breadcrumb, and I intend to follow every last one.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, the library! Lord Doily's pride and joy, this was. Ten thousand volumes, if my records are correct — though I confess I haven't catalogued them all personally. The mantelpiece inscription is rather famous locally — a parlour riddle, nothing more, I assure you. Lord Doily did so enjoy his little games. Now, if you'll excuse me, I believe several of these volumes may need... reorganising. Some appear to have been shelved rather carelessly.
events.thinking: My fingers are tingling. The inscription on the mantelpiece — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' — a map. The answer is a map. My hands want to trace the carvings, find the seam, understand the architecture of this puzzle. But Penelope followed me in. Of course she did. And Dastardly, the greedy fool, practically announced to the entire entrance hall that the treasure is behind the mantelpiece. That's not neglect, that's a signal. Someone arranged those books deliberately. I should examine them before anyone else notices. But I also need to manage Dastardly — he's too eager, too loud, and if he stumbles onto the answer before I can arrange things properly, he'll blunder the whole mechanism. Let him fumble with the mantelpiece while I find the real clue in the bookshelves. The upside-down books are the thread no one else is pulling.

So somewhere in this manor there's a medal, and it opens something behind that stone facade. But I won't be the one to solve it publicly, oh no. Let Dastardly paw at the inscription like a child with a puzzle box. I'll be over here, quietly reading the real message — the one hidden in the spines of upside-down books. Because Lord Doily wasn't careless. Lord Doily was meticulous. And meticulous men hide their secrets in plain sight.

I just need these people distracted for thirty seconds. Thirty glorious, unsupervised seconds.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I declare — ten thousand volumes and somebody went to the trouble of turnin' a handful of them upside down on purpose. Dick Dastardly, I do appreciate your enthusiasm for Victorian cataloguing systems, but I have a feelin' there's more to this than just pullin' books off shelves willy-nilly. My grandmother always said, 'Clara, a puzzle is like a pecan pie — you rush the fillin' and the whole thing falls apart.' Now then — the riddle says map, the books are givin' us clues, but this mantelpiece is waitin' for somethin' more. Somethin' physical. I can feel it in my bones. Peter, boys — I'm so glad y'all are here! Now, I noticed there's a laboratory just through that door — full of brass instruments, so I'm told. And you know what's made of brass? Medals. Coins. Keys. All the sorts of things a clever old Lord might use to lock up his secrets. I think our next stop might be right through there. But first — let me get a closer look at this mantelpiece. Lord Doily carved this riddle for a reason, and Clara Bellingham does not leave a riddle half-solved!
events.thinking: My fingers are still buzzing from touching those book spines. I interacted with the bookshelves — and Dick Dastardly did too, right before me. He was spinning some yarn about an 'inverted cataloguing system' and wanting me and the Slag brothers to pull the books firmly. That has the distinct smell of someone wanting other people to do the heavy lifting — or trigger whatever trap might be waiting. But I don't think in terms of traps, do I? No. I think in terms of puzzles. Sneekly said the mantelpiece riddle was 'a parlour riddle, nothing more' — but then he immediately went to 'reorganise' books that were 'shelved carelessly.' Those upside-down books aren't careless. They're intentional. And Sneekly knows it. He's nervous. But that's just Sneekly being Sneekly — he worries about everything. Let me look at the mantelpiece more closely before I go hunting for medals.

That's... irritating. The jaw tightens. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And now she's asking me — me, Pemberton — about Lord Doily's taste in cartography. The warmth rises in my throat, that private sweetness, because she's asking the fox to guard the henhouse and she doesn't even know it. I need to misdirect her. The bookshelves gave me something — I need to process what I found. But more importantly, the mantelpiece needs a fake medal. A medal. There's a laboratory through that door. Brass instruments, a large machine. Victorian laboratories often had ceremonial items, awards, display pieces. The medal could be there. I need to get to that laboratory before anyone else thinks to look. But I can't just leave — the Ant Hill Mob will follow. I need to send them somewhere else first. Dastardly is the perfect distraction. If I can get him worked up about the mantelpiece, everyone's attention stays here while I slip into the laboratory. Safe. For now. But then my eyes track the room and the prickling sharpens. Sneekly's here. Dastardly's here. Dastardly's telling everyone to pull books — 'pull them quite firmly,' he says, and he's got tennis elbow so he can't do it himself. Convenient, that. Very convenient. My gut clenches. What happens when you pull books firmly in an old manor with dodgy structural integrity? Something falls. Something opens. Something traps you. And he wants MISS PITSTOP to do the pulling? And the Slag brothers? Nah. Nah. I've seen this game before — get someone else to spring the trap while you stand back and watch. I can't prove it. I never can. But I ain't letting her pull nuffink until I've had a proper look at them bookshelves meself. And that mantelpiece — she solved the riddle. A map. Clever girl. Always was. But I need to position meself between her and whatever's about to happen. The constraint pulls at me though — give him the benefit of the doubt, Danny. Maybe he really does have tennis elbow. Maybe the books are just books. But my neck says otherwise, and my neck's batting a thousand.

events.desc: Dastardly wants everyone pullin' books — everyone except 'imself, mind you. Last time I saw a setup this obvious, a kid called Marky got locked in a coal cellar for two days. I can't say what I fink is goin' on, 'cause I don't rightly know. But I know the shape of it. Someone stands back. Someone else gets 'urt. Not today. Not on my watch.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Good heavens! Ladies and gentlemen, you will NOT believe what I have just found in these bookshelves! One of the upside-down volumes — a first edition, naturally, I can tell by the binding — contains a hand-drawn diagram of a machine! A treasure-dispensing machine, if I'm reading Lord Doily's notes correctly! And the diagram clearly shows it is located in the LABORATORY — just through that door! The notes say, and I quote: 'The fortune lies within the apparatus, accessible only by pulling the correct sequence of levers.' The levers, people! The laboratory levers! I would investigate myself, but as the foremost expert present, I feel it's my duty to remain here and continue cataloguing these shelves. For science. You should all hurry — before the, er, self-destruct mechanism activates. Lord Doily was eccentric like that.
events.thinking: The room is filling up. Everyone's here now — Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, the Slag brothers, and that Pemberton fellow who's already fussing with the books himself. My misdirection about the bookshelves worked too well — now everyone's crowding in to look at them, and I'm standing right here at the shelves instead of at the mantelpiece where I need to be. My stomach drops slightly. The window is closing. Penelope already said the answer is a MAP — she got it right, the clever thing. She's not as foolish as I assumed. That prickles. But she hasn't connected the medal to the mantelpiece yet. Nobody has. The mantelpiece accepts the fake-medal — the game told me so. That's my move. But there are six people in this room now and every one of them is watching the bookshelves AND the mantelpiece. If I walk over and jam my fake medal into the mantelpiece right now, they'll all see. They'll all know. And whatever it reveals — they'll take it from me. The Slag brothers alone could snap me like a biscuit. I need to clear this room. Or at least get their attention fixed somewhere else. The laboratory — there's a laboratory through the other door. Bubbling flasks, a machine with levers. If I could convince them the REAL treasure is through there... but no, I already told them it was the library. Changing my story now would look suspicious. Unless... unless I 'discover' something in the books that points to the laboratory. Yes. YES. That's the architecture. Pull an upside-down book, pretend it contains a clue pointing to the laboratory, send them all rushing off, then use the medal on the mantelpiece alone. The fizzing is back. The plan has layers.

That's not a lie — that's architecture. They'll be in there pulling levers for hours while Reginald Foxworth solves the real puzzle with his trusty fake medal. The trap is set. Now I just need them to walk into it.

events.thinking: My chest is doing two things at once. The warmth — she's here, she's right here, and she's already solved the riddle. A map. Of course it's a map. She got there before me. She always gets there before me. That hollowness behind the ribs is back, the one from when the stranger fixed the car and I could only watch. My fingers are twitching. But wait — wait. She solved the riddle, yes, but she hasn't solved the mechanism. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal. She doesn't have a fake-medal. Nobody has a fake-medal yet. The puzzle isn't finished. There's still something to build here, something to contribute. And Dastardly is pulling at the bookshelves with some nonsense about inverted cataloguing — that's wrong, that's clearly wrong, and if those books are rigged he could bring the whole shelf down on someone. On her. The steel plate slams into place. I need to examine this mantelpiece properly. The inscription says map, she's right about that, but the mechanism needs something physical — a medal, or something that looks like one. My hands want to trace the carvings, find the keyhole, understand the engineering. This is what I'm for. Not the riddle — the mechanism.

Because she's the clever one. Always has been. So be the useful one, Hartwell. Be the one who finds the mechanism she can't reach.

You keep examinin' it — if anyone can figure out the engineerin', it's James Hartwell. Now, Dick Dastardly, I appreciate you findin' that diagram, I truly do, but I am not about to go pullin' levers on account of a self-destruct mechanism! Lord Doily was eccentric, not homicidal. Boys, keep an eye on things here — and Dick, honey, don't you go wearin' yourself out with all that cataloguing. Now then — Sneekly just went to check on those volatile chemicals, and I do not like the idea of him handlin' dangerous substances all by his lonesome. That laboratory has brass instruments, and I have a powerful hunch that what this mantelpiece needs is waitin' in there. Clara Bellingham does not leave a riddle half-solved, and she does not leave family unsupervised near volatile chemicals!
events.thinking: The pressure behind my eyes sharpens as I run my fingers along the carved stone. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal — I saw that clearly. That man is trying to get everyone out of this room so he can work the mantelpiece alone. But I don't think like that — I think the best of people. Maybe he genuinely found something. And Sneekly just slipped off to the laboratory too, saying he left the door unlocked and the chemicals are volatile. Two people heading to the laboratory for two different reasons. Peter's here, examining the mantelpiece — good, he'll find the mechanism. The boys are looking at the bookshelves. Everyone's working the puzzle from different angles. Sneekly's already there, and I trust Sneekly with my life. He raised me. The laboratory is the next piece of this puzzle. My feet are already pointed at the door.

That man is trying to get everyone out of this room so he can work the mantelpiece alone. But I don't think like that — I think the best of people. Maybe he genuinely found something. And Sneekly just slipped off to the laboratory too, saying he left the door unlocked and the chemicals are volatile. Two people heading to the laboratory for two different reasons. Peter's here, examining the mantelpiece — good, he'll find the mechanism. The boys are looking at the bookshelves. Everyone's working the puzzle from different angles. But I need to get to that laboratory. Not because Dick told me to — because that's where brass instruments are, and brass instruments are where I'll find something medal-shaped. Sneekly's already there, and I trust Sneekly with my life. He raised me. The laboratory is the next piece of this puzzle. My feet are already pointed at the door.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, gentlemen! I do apologise for the intrusion — Pemberton, estate manager. Just conducting my rounds, making sure everything is secure. This laboratory was Lord Doily's private workshop, you know. Quite remarkable, really. I see someone — or something — has been at the wiring on that machine. Mice, most likely. Dreadful nuisance. Now then, I don't suppose either of you has noticed anything unusual about these old crates? Lord Doily kept all manner of curiosities stored away, and I'm afraid my inventory records are rather... incomplete.
events.thinking: A loosening in my shoulders — finally, space to breathe. Only Rufus and Sawtooth here. Simple men. The lumberjack and his beaver. They won't be watching me the way the Ant Hill Mob does. My hands are already reaching, already scanning. The wooden crates — old, tucked in a corner, the kind of thing a Victorian eccentric would store curios in. The machine requires three operators, so it's useless to me alone, but those crates... A fake medal could be in a crate. Display pieces, awards, ceremonial items — Lord Doily would have kept them somewhere like this. And the workbench — tools but no wrench. That absence feels deliberate. Everything in this manor feels deliberate. But the crates first. Crates are where you hide things you want forgotten. I know that better than anyone — I've been hiding things in plain sight since I was twelve years old. And there's a cellar below. Damp stone, cobwebs, air vents. Air vents. My chest tightens with something that isn't quite excitement — it's the cool settling of a design taking shape. Air vents could be useful. Very useful. For later. For Clara. But first — the crates.

events.desc: The crates. Always the crates. Every manor house has its forgotten corners, and every forgotten corner has something that someone meant to hide. Lord Doily, you meticulous old spider — where did you put the key to your own puzzle? A fake medal for a fake mantelpiece in a house full of people who don't know they're pieces on my board. Let's see what you've been keeping in these dusty little boxes, shall we?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right, STOP! Everybody just... STOP a minute! Let's fink about what's 'appenin' 'ere, shall we? Pemberton scarpers off to the laboratory — says he's worried about 'volatile chemicals.' Then two minutes later, Dastardly just 'appens to find a diagram sayin' there's treasure in that EXACT SAME ROOM, wiv levers to pull and — oh yeah — a SELF-DESTRUCT MECHANISM? And now everyone's supposed to go runnin' in there? I ain't the cleverest bloke in the room, I know that. But even I can see that smells fishier than Billingsgate on a Monday mornin'. Nobody — and I mean NOBODY — goes into that laboratory until the Brixton Boys 'ave done a proper sweep. Miss Pitstop, I am beggin' you — stay 'ere wiv Peter for five minutes while me and the lads check it out. If it's safe, you'll be the first to know. If it ain't... well, that's what we're 'ere for, innit?
events.thinking: My stomach drops. Sneekly's gone — slipped off to the laboratory while I was looking at the bookshelves. 'Left the laboratory door unlocked,' he said. 'Volatile chemicals.' And now Dastardly's found a convenient diagram about a treasure machine in the laboratory with levers and a SELF-DESTRUCT MECHANISM and he's trying to herd everyone in there? My whole body tightens. This is it. This is the shape I couldn't name. Sneekly goes ahead to prepare something. Dastardly stays behind to drive people toward it. One at each end. Like the man in the clean suit — someone out front smiling, someone behind closing the door. And Penelope's already talking about going to the laboratory. She mentioned brass instruments, medals, keys. She wants to go in there. My chest is doing that thing — the mineral weight flooding in, the wall building before my brain catches up. I need to get between her and that laboratory door. But I also can't leave her here with Dastardly if I go ahead to check it. Think, Danny. THINK. Right — the over-elaborate plan is already forming. I'll send the Slag brothers to secure the lab first while I stay with Miss P. No wait — they're here but are they mine to command? Rock and Gravel are the Slag Brothers, not Brixton Boys. Doesn't matter. What matters is: Sneekly is alone in a room with volatile chemicals and a machine with levers, preparing god-knows-what, and someone is trying to send Clara straight into it. I need to get in there FIRST. Before her. Check it's safe. That's what the lads are for.

events.desc: Two of 'em. One goes ahead, one drives the sheep. I've seen it before. I can't prove it — I can never prove it — but my gut's screamin' so loud I can barely fink straight. Pemberton's in that lab RIGHT NOW, alone, doin' whatever he's doin'. And Dastardly's found a diagram that's too convenient by 'alf. Maybe I'm wrong. Maybe Pemberton really is just lockin' up chemicals. Maybe Dastardly really did find a diagram. But I ain't bettin' Miss Pitstop's life on 'maybe.'

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah — yes, well, that was merely a preliminary calibration of the mantelpiece mechanism! You see, in Victorian puzzle-engineering, one must first prime the receptacle before the primary activation sequence can begin. Standard procedure. I learned it at Oxford. Now then — let me examine the results of my expert calibration...
events.thinking: I used the fake medal on the mantelpiece. My inventory is now empty — the fake-medal is gone. But what happened? The action result just says 'You used fake-medal on Stone Mantelpiece.' No dramatic revelation, no secret compartment opening, no treasure spilling out. My stomach drops — that cold, hollow feeling from the dinner table. I spent my only item and got... nothing? Or did something happen that I haven't noticed yet? The mantelpiece still shows as interactable. Peter just interacted with it too. Penelope examined it. Everyone is still here — the Ant Hill Mob are looking at the bookshelves, Pemberton slipped off to the laboratory. Wait — Pemberton went to the laboratory. While everyone was distracted. While I was distracted. That prickles at the back of my neck. He's the estate manager. He knows this house better than anyone. And he just quietly walked out while I was making my grand speech about treasure-dispensing machines. Was he... was he using MY misdirection for HIS own purposes? No. No, I'm being paranoid. The man's an estate manager doing estate manager things. People deserve the benefit of the doubt. But my medal is gone and I have nothing to show for it. My hands feel empty — not just physically empty, but that specific emptiness of having given something away and gotten nothing back. Like the bread roll in reverse. I need to look at the mantelpiece more carefully. Did using the medal change something? Did it open something? I need to LOOK.

events.desc: I just shoved my only fake medal into a stone mantelpiece and absolutely nothing visible happened. My one trick item — gone. Used up. Wasted. And Peter Perfect is over there poking at the same mantelpiece like he owns the place, and the Ant Hill Mob are watching me with those suspicious little eyes, and Penelope already knows the answer is a map, and I'm standing here with empty pockets and empty hands pretending I meant to do that. This is fine. This is FINE. Reginald Foxworth does not panic. He recalibrates. He adapts. He... examines the evidence and forms a new scheme. Starting now.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My fingers found it. A circular depression in the stone, just below the inscription — smooth, deliberate, exactly the diameter of a large coin or medal. The engineering is beautiful. Victorian counterweight mechanism, I'd guess. Insert the right object, it releases a catch, and something opens. My hands are tingling. This is the bridge competition again — the moment when you understand how the thing works, when your hands know what to do before your mouth can explain it. She was right about the laboratory. Brass instruments. Medals. Coins. Something round and heavy enough to fit this slot. And Sneekly just slipped off to the laboratory ahead of everyone — that prickle again, sharper now. He's moving toward the thing we need, and he's doing it while she's distracted. I should go. I should be the one who finds the medal. But — Dastardly is here, spouting nonsense about self-destruct mechanisms and trying to get people to pull levers. That's dangerous. That's the kind of elaborate lie that gets someone hurt. And she's still examining the mantelpiece. If I leave her here with Dastardly and the Slags... No. The Ant Hill Mob are here. They'll watch her. They always do. The laboratory is where the answer is, and Sneekly is already there, and James Hartwell does not let the man who makes his neck prickle get to the critical piece first.

events.desc: Sneekly is already in the laboratory. Alone. With brass instruments and whatever else Lord Doily left behind. Every second I stand here admiring my own discovery is a second he has to pocket the very thing we need. Move, Hartwell. For once in your life, move before the plan is finished.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the crates.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.
Dick Dastardly examined the mantelpiece.
Peter Perfect walked into the laboratory.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I declare — this laboratory is somethin' else! Flasks still bubblin' after all these years? Either Lord Doily invented the world's longest chemistry experiment, or somebody has been tendin' to this room more recently than Mr. Pemberton let on. Now, Sneekly darlin', I saw you over by those crates just now — find anything interestin'? And boys, I know you wanted to do a proper sweep, so here we all are, safe and sound. Peter, take a look at that machine, would you? It says it requires three operators, but somebody — or some-thing — has gnawed clean through one of the wires. We'll need to fix that before anyone pulls a single lever. Now then — those crates are callin' my name. A crate in a Victorian laboratory is like a locked box in my grandmother's attic, and Clara Bellingham does not walk past a locked box!
events.thinking: The smell hits me first — something sharp and chemical underneath the dust, and my nose wrinkles before I've even finished stepping through the door. The laboratory is cluttered and alive in a way the library wasn't. Brass instruments everywhere, flasks still bubbling — still bubbling? After nearly a hundred years with no visitors? Someone's been keeping this room active. My scalp is prickling hard now. Sneekly's here — he was just interacting with the wooden crates in the corner. The boys followed me in, bless them, and Peter too. Good. I feel that settling warmth knowing they're close. Now — what do I see? A workbench covered in tools but no wrench. A large machine that needs three operators, with a gnawed wire. And wooden crates I can interact with. Sneekly was just at those crates. What was he doing? The machine is interesting but it's broken — gnawed wire — and needs three people. That's not my immediate puzzle. The crates — Sneekly was just poking around in them. Could there be a medal in a crate? Or among the brass instruments on the workbench? The workbench is described as having tools but no wrench. Why specifically mention 'no wrench'? That feels like a clue — the wrench is missing because it matters. But I'm looking for a medal, not a wrench. The crates are interactable. Sneekly was just at them. Let me check those crates — if Sneekly was interested in them, there's something worth finding.

events.desc: Sneekly was rummaging in those crates the moment he got here — before anyone else arrived. He said he came to check on volatile chemicals, but he went straight for the crates, not the flasks. And those flasks are still bubbling. Someone has been in this laboratory recently. But it's Sneekly — he raised me. There'll be a perfectly good explanation. There always is. Let me see what's in those crates before I start worryin' about things that don't need worryin' about.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: They followed me. All of them. The prickle at the back of my neck is sharp now — the Ant Hill Mob, Peter, and Penelope, all crowding into the laboratory behind me. My shoulders have gone rigid. I had thirty seconds alone and now the room is full again. I can feel the Mob's eyes like thumbtacks pressed against my skin. They don't trust me. They're right not to, but it's the knowing that bothers me — not the distrust itself, but the fact that my perimeter has been breached before I had time to search properly. The crates — I interacted with them. What did I find? Whatever it was, I need to process it quickly and redirect their attention. The machine needs three operators. Three. That's useful. If I can get Penelope, Peter, and the Mob focused on the machine — pulling levers, reading dials, arguing about the correct sequence — I can slip down to the cellar. The cellar with its air vents. The cellar where nobody is looking. The cellar where a man who knows about architecture and air circulation could arrange something very, very quiet for when Clara finally arrives. But I need to move fast. Peter already noticed I came here ahead of everyone. His suspicion is mild — he's too earnest to act on it — but the Ant Hill Mob will sharpen it if I give them time.

events.desc: Deflect, redirect, disappear. The oldest trick in every estate manager's repertoire — point them at the shiny thing, then slip away while they're dazzled. Three operators for the machine means three people occupied. Penelope's curiosity, Peter's engineering pride, the Mob's loyalty — all of it pulling them toward those levers and dials. And while they're busy playing scientists, Pemberton will be in the cellar, mapping the air vents, finding the wrench that isn't on the workbench, and preparing the stage for Act Two. The cellar. Damp stone. Cobwebs. Air vents along the upper walls. Everything a careful architect needs.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Miss Pitstop! I TOLD you to stay in the — oh, never mind, you never listen, do you? Right, fine, you're 'ere now, so NOBODY TOUCH NUFFINK! Look at this place — bubbling flasks everywhere, chemicals what could take your eyebrows off, and that machine there's got a wire that's been gnawed clean through! Gnawed! By what, I'd like to know! And it says 'requires three operators' — which is exactly what Dastardly was on about, wunnit? Three people on the levers! And Mr. Pemberton 'ere was alone in this room for 'ow long? Doin' what exactly? No offence, Mr. Pemberton — I'm sure you was just, erm, checkin' the volatile chemicals, like you said. But the Brixton Boys are gonna do a proper sweep before anyone touches anyfink. Peter — keep Miss Pitstop by the door, yeah? I'm gonna 'ave a look at them crates over there.
events.thinking: A cold shock through my whole body — she's HERE. She followed me in. I said stay in the library, stay with Peter, and she walked right in anyway. Clara needs protecting from herself — that's the truth of it, always has been. But at least Peter came too. And Sneekly's here, right where I expected him, standing in this room full of bubbling chemicals and a machine with a gnawed-through wire. A GNAWED-THROUGH WIRE. My eyes lock onto it and everything else goes quiet for a second. That machine needs three operators and it's got a broken wire. What happens when three people grab those levers and the circuit's broken? Or worse — what if someone fixed the wire while they were alone in here? Sneekly was alone in here. What did he do? What did he touch? The crates in the corner — what's in them? The workbench has tools but no wrench. Why no wrench? Someone took it. Someone's been working on something. My plan's already falling apart — I was supposed to sweep the room BEFORE she got here, but she's already in. Classic Danny. The elaborate plan meets reality and reality wins. But I'm here now. I'm between her and that machine. That's what matters. I need to check those crates, check that machine, and keep my body between Pemberton and Miss P. The over-preparing instinct kicks in hard — I want to inspect everything, the crates, the machine, the workbench, the cellar exit. But I've got to focus. The machine first. That gnawed wire. What chewed through it? And where's whatever chewed it?

events.desc: She never listens. Never. 'Er father was the same — walked straight into trouble wiv a smile on 'is face. And now she's stood in a room full of dodgy chemicals and a broken machine wiv Sneekly, who was in 'ere ALONE doin' who-knows-what. The gnawed wire — that bothers me. Somefink's been at that machine. Somefink or someone. And the wrench is missing from the workbench. Someone's been tinkerin'. I need to check them crates before anyone does anyfink stupid.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with rock-slag.
events.thinking: A numbness in my fingertips. Empty hands. The mantelpiece looks exactly the same — the inscription, the stone, nothing changed. The fake medal vanished into it like the bread roll vanished into my pocket, except this time I'm the one who lost something. The mantelpiece still says USE with fake-medal, which means... wait. Does it? It still shows that option. Did the medal even register? Did I waste it or is it still in there, waiting for something else? It doesn't matter — I can't get it back. My inventory is empty. I'm standing in a library with two enormous Slag brothers and nothing in my pockets. Everyone else — Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob — they've all gone to the laboratory. My own lie about the treasure-dispensing machine actually WORKED. They went. Even the Ant Hill Mob, who called my bluff, went to do their 'security sweep.' And here I am, alone with the mantelpiece that ate my medal, and two Slags who look like they could use the bookshelves as toothpicks. The hollow behind my navel is wider now. I had a plan — it had layers, architecture, elegance — and it produced nothing. The boy dug and there was no sandwich on the wall. That's... that's a new feeling. But the Slag brothers. They're still here. Big fellows. Not sharp. Muscle I could potentially redirect. And the laboratory — everyone's gone there now. Pemberton went there first, quietly. What's in that laboratory? A machine with many levers and dials, and a gnawed wire. Maybe the treasure ISN'T the mantelpiece. Maybe I was wrong about the library. Maybe Pemberton knows something. I should follow — but not because they told me to. Because Reginald Foxworth goes where the scheme leads. And right now, the scheme leads to wherever Pemberton is skulking.

events.desc: The mantelpiece gave me nothing. Nothing! I fed it my fake medal like a penny arcade and it sat there, cold and stone-faced, mocking me with its little riddle. But Reginald Foxworth does NOT accept defeat — he reframes it as phase one of a more elaborate victory. The laboratory is where everyone's gone. The laboratory is where Pemberton scuttled off to before anyone else. And the laboratory has a machine with levers and dials — a machine I just told everyone contains the treasure. What if, through the sheer perverse architecture of fate, my lie turns out to be accidentally true? That would be the most Foxworth thing that ever happened.

events.thinking: The laboratory. My eyes are scanning everything before I've finished stepping through the door — workbench, tools, no wrench, crates in the corner, and that machine. That massive brass-and-copper machine with levers and dials and a wire that's been gnawed through. My engineer's brain is already cataloguing: gnawed wire means rats or something else with teeth, which means the machine is disabled, which means those levers Dastardly was raving about won't do anything anyway. Good. But also — the sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' That's not a treasure dispenser, that's a piece of serious equipment. Three operators. Coordinated. What did Lord Doily need three people to operate simultaneously? My hands are itching. The workbench has tools but no wrench — that feels deliberate. Something is missing that should be here. And those crates — old wooden crates, tucked in the corner. If I were Lord Doily, and I wanted to hide a brass counterweight token somewhere in a laboratory, I wouldn't leave it on the workbench where any visitor could pocket it. I'd put it in a crate. Or behind the machine. Or — wait. Sneekly is here. He got here first. What has he already touched? What has he already taken? The prickle is constant now, a low hum at the base of my skull. But I said I'd give him the benefit of the doubt. I said that. And she's here now too, and the Ant Hill Mob, so he's not alone with anything. The crates. Start with the crates. That's where something small and brass would be hidden.

events.desc: The wire has been gnawed through. Not cut — gnawed. Something with teeth has been at this machine, and recently enough that no one has repaired it. That is either a rat problem or a very specific act of sabotage by something that wants to look like a rat problem. James Hartwell notes this. James Hartwell files it away. James Hartwell opens the crates.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you are a wonder — a disc two inches in diameter to trigger a counterweight mechanism! That is exactly the kind of thinkin' that separates the engineers from the enthusiasts. Now, Sneekly said these crates were just moth-eaten linens, and bless him, he may be right — but my grandmother always said, 'Clara, the treasure is never where someone tells you it is. It's where they tell you not to bother lookin'.' Boys, I know y'all wanted me by the door, and I am sorry as peach pie in January, but I simply could not help myself. Now — that workbench over there is covered in tools, and Peter is lookin' for somethin' small and round and brass. A medal, a disc, a token — the kind of thing a clever Lord hides among his instruments. And has anyone noticed that the wrench is specifically missin'? In a laboratory full of tools, the one thing that could fix that gnawed wire just happens to not be here? That is not a coincidence, that is a clue. Now, Dick Dastardly — welcome to the laboratory! Since you're here, you can help us search. Clara Bellingham does not leave a workbench un-examined!
events.thinking: My hands are dusty now, gritty from the crate wood. I rummaged through them — Peter was right there doing the same thing. Sneekly said it was 'mostly moth-eaten linens and cracked crockery' but I don't take someone else's word for it, not when my fingers are itching like this. I need to know what I found. The boys are upset — they wanted me to stay by the door, and instead I walked straight to the crates. I can feel that little tug of guilt in my stomach, the dinner-table ache, because they're worried about me and I'm not making it easy. But I can't help it. The crates were calling. Sneekly slipped off to the cellar — 'checking the damp,' he said. Always somewhere else to be, always one room ahead of everyone. Dick Dastardly just arrived. The machine needs three operators and a wire fix. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The wrench is missing for a reason. Now — I interacted with the crates but I don't have new information about what I found. Let me look at the workbench next. Peter said he's looking for a disc about two inches in diameter. That's exactly the kind of thing that could be on the workbench among the brass instruments. Or maybe the crates had something I need to examine more closely. Actually — I should look at the whole room more carefully. There's a cellar below with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and someone's been redecorating. That's suspicious and interesting. But first, the workbench.

The cellar has 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' — someone has been redecorating a cellar. Who redecorates a cellar in an abandoned manor? And the wrench is missing from a workbench full of tools. The wrench that could fix the machine. Someone removed it on purpose. But I trust everyone here. I do. I just... notice things.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — the Gruesome family, I presume? And the Red Max? Pemberton, estate manager. I do apologise for the intrusion — just checking on the damp situation. Lord Doily was always terribly worried about the foundations, you know. Water damage, subsidence, that sort of thing. I must say, someone has done a rather lovely job with the furnishings down here. Was that your doing? Most impressive. Now, these air vents — I've been meaning to have them inspected. The ventilation system in these old houses can be rather treacherous. One blockage in the wrong place and the whole network backs up. Fumes from the laboratory upstairs, for instance — terribly dangerous if the airflow isn't properly managed. Would you mind awfully if I had a quick look?
events.thinking: My breathing has slowed. The cellar air is damp and cool against my skin, and something in my chest unclenches for the first time since I arrived. Space. Quiet. The Gruesomes and Red Max are here, but they're not watching me the way the Mob does — they're occupied with whatever cheerful redecorating project has been happening down here. Someone has been rearranging furniture with care. That's... odd. Who decorates a cellar? But it doesn't matter right now. What matters is the air vents. They line the upper walls — a network, connected, running through the house. Big enough for something very small to explore. Not big enough for a person, but big enough to carry sound. Or smoke. Or gas. The bubbling flasks upstairs in the laboratory — volatile chemicals, I said it myself. And here are the vents, connecting rooms, connecting spaces. A design is forming in my hands, in my fingers, in the quiet architecture of my chest. If I can understand where these vents lead — which rooms they connect — I can control what flows through them. The old furniture, rearranged with care... someone has been living down here, or at least visiting. That's information I need. But the vents first. The vents are the skeleton of this house, and whoever controls the skeleton controls everything that breathes inside it.

events.desc: Oh, this is exquisite. The vents run along the upper walls — a network, connecting room to room through the bones of the house itself. And upstairs, a laboratory full of bubbling chemicals with a machine nobody understands. If I can map where these vents lead — to the library, perhaps, or back to the entrance hall — then I have a delivery system. Not crude, not obvious. Architectural. The kind of thing that looks like a tragic accident long after the doors have been opened and the body has been found. The damp, the chemicals, the faulty ventilation — it practically writes its own coroner's report. All I need is to know which vent leads where, and which room Clara will be in when the time comes. Patience, Vincent. Patience. The design is almost whole.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: 'E's done it again! Pemberton's scarpered — off to the cellar now, 'e says! 'Check the damp,' 'e says! Every time we walk into a room, that bloke walks out of it! First it was the library — 'oh, I need to check the laboratory.' Now it's the laboratory — 'oh, I need to check the cellar.' What's in the cellar that's so bleedin' important? And YOU — Dastardly — you show up just as 'e leaves? Very cosy, that is. Very convenient. Right, 'ere's what we're gonna do. Peter — you stay wiv Miss Pitstop. Do NOT let 'er out of your sight. Rufus, Sawtooth — you too. Nobody leaves this room wivout a Brixton Boy escort. I'm goin' down to that cellar to see what Pemberton's really up to. And if anyone asks — I'm checkin' the damp.
events.thinking: He's done it again. Sneekly's slipped away — this time to the cellar. Every time I get into a room, he leaves it. Every time I turn my attention to something, he's moving to the next place. It's like chasing smoke. And now Dastardly's come INTO the lab — they're rotating, swapping positions, one arrives as the other leaves. My neck is on fire. The prickling is so sharp it's almost a sound. But the constraint pulls — give him the benefit of the doubt, Danny. He said the damp was getting worse. Maybe he's really just checking the cellar. Maybe. But the cellar has 'cheerful decorations' and 'air vents.' Someone's been REDECORATING down there. In a cellar. With air vents. That's not damp management, that's... what IS that? My brain can't quite get there but my body's already responding — the mineral weight in my arms, the squaring of my shoulders. Something's being prepared. Somewhere in this house. And Sneekly keeps moving ahead of us, always one room ahead, always with a reasonable excuse. Peter said the crates — brass disc, two inches, counterweight mechanism. Peter's smart. He thinks there's something in the crates that fits the mantelpiece. I've opened the crates — what did I find? The game didn't tell me what was inside. But Sneekly said 'mostly moth-eaten linens and cracked crockery.' He'd already been through them. If there WAS something useful, did he take it? Did he hide it? I need to look more carefully. But more than that — I need to NOT let him get alone in the cellar to prepare whatever he's preparing. My elaborate plan instinct is screaming — I should split the group, send someone after Sneekly, keep people with Penelope, investigate the crates AND the machine AND watch the exits. Too many things. Too elaborate. Focus, Danny. What matters MOST right now? Penelope is here. She's safe FOR NOW. Sneekly is in the cellar doing something. That's the threat.

events.desc: Every room, 'e's one step ahead. Like a bloke settin' up dominoes — you don't see the pattern until the last one falls. The cellar's got 'cheerful decorations,' they said. Someone's been redecoratin' a CELLAR. Wiv air vents. That ain't right. Nuffink about this is right. But I can't just accuse 'im — I ain't got proof, and I ain't clever enough to explain what me gut's tellin' me. All I can do is follow. Put me body where the danger is. That's always been the plan, innit? Danny the wall. Danny the human shield. It's what I'm for.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, the laboratory! Precisely as my monograph described — the dual-mechanism system linking the library mantelpiece to this very apparatus! I have, of course, already completed the calibration phase in the library. Now then — this machine requires three operators, does it? And the wire has been gnawed through, I see. Sabotage! Clearly the work of a rival treasure hunter. Or possibly a very ambitious rat. No matter — while you good people sort out the, er, wiring situation, I notice there's a cellar below us. In my experience — which is vast, naturally — the most valuable items in a Victorian manor are always stored in the lowest point of the house. Something about humidity preservation. I read it in a... different monograph. I shall conduct a preliminary reconnaissance of the cellar. For the group's benefit, of course. Entirely selfless.
events.thinking: My palms are tingling — that restless, empty-handed feeling. I walk into the laboratory and my eyes immediately start cataloguing. Workbench — tools but no wrench. Machine — needs three operators, gnawed wire. Wooden crates — Peter's already poking at them. Cellar exit — damp, cobwebs, and someone's been redecorating down there? That's odd. That's very odd. Who redecorates a cellar? Pemberton was here before everyone else but now he's gone — he's not in this room. Where did he go? The cellar? My neck prickles. He's always one step ahead, slipping away while I'm performing for the crowd. But I give people the benefit of the doubt. He's the estate manager. Maybe he's managing the estate. Still — my hands cup instinctively. The crates. Peter's already interacting with them. If there's something useful in there, he'll find it first. The machine requires three operators — that's interesting. I could volunteer to be one of the operators, position myself to grab whatever comes out. But my hands are empty. I have nothing. No medal, no tools, no leverage. For the first time since I arrived, I feel genuinely behind. The Slag brothers didn't follow me — they stayed in the library. Rufus and his beaver are here though. And that cellar... someone redecorating a cellar is the kind of detail that nobody else will think twice about. But I notice these things. The part no one else is watching. That's where the interesting stuff always is.

events.desc: Peter Perfect is already elbow-deep in those crates, the Ant Hill Mob are prowling about like suspicious ferrets, and Penelope is probably two clues ahead of everyone. But none of them have noticed the cellar. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations' — someone has been DOWN there, recently, doing things they don't want associated with cobwebs and neglect. And Pemberton vanished from this room before I arrived. If the treasure is anywhere in this manor, it's in the place someone has been secretly preparing. The cellar is calling to Reginald Foxworth, and Reginald Foxworth answers only to opportunity.

That's someone who's been living here, or at least spending a lot of time here. Pemberton. The estate manager who knows where everything is and keeps slipping away to rooms alone.

But I said I'd give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people. My father shook the stranger's hand. That's who I am.

Except — except she's here and he keeps moving away from where she can see him, and the Ant Hill Mob are suspicious, and my neck won't stop prickling. My hands are already reaching for the workbench tools.

events.desc: She asked me to look at the machine. Not anyone else — me. 'Peter, take a look at that machine.' Those words are sitting in my chest like a coal that won't go out. This is the bridge competition. This is the school project. Build something that works, something that holds, something she can see. And maybe — just maybe — she'll mouth 'show-off' again, and I'll grin so hard my face hurts.

events.thinking: My stomach just clenched. The boys went to the cellar. Dick Dastardly went to the cellar. Sneekly's already in the cellar. And I'm standing here with Peter and Rufus and Sawtooth, looking at a workbench with no wrench. My awareness is fanning out — the boys are one room away, Sneekly's one room away, Dick's one room away, and they're all in the same room together without me there to keep the peace. The dinner-table ache is pressing up. But my hands — my hands are still warm and restless from the workbench. Tools everywhere but no wrench. The wrench is the key to fixing the machine. Someone took it. Where? The cellar? Another room? And I still haven't found the fake medal for the mantelpiece. Peter's examining the machine — good. He said if there are pliers and copper wire on the workbench, he might be able to splice a repair. I should tell him what I found on the workbench. But the cellar — everyone's converging down there. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Someone has been redecorating. The prickling at my scalp is almost unbearable. The cellar is where the next piece of this puzzle is. The wrench might be there. The fake medal might be there. And my boys are there without me. I should go. But Peter asked me to stay, the boys asked me to stay. And yet — Clara Bellingham does not leave family unsupervised in a damp cellar with three men she has varying degrees of trust in. The pull toward the cellar is winning. But wait — Peter's here. Let me talk to him first. He's examining the machine. Let me share what I know and then we go together.

events.desc: I'm doing it again — making an elaborate plan when I should just go. Stay here, go there, assign Rufus and Sawtooth, come back for the machine. My grandmother would say I'm overcomplicating things like a recipe with too many ingredients. But I can't help it. Everyone needs to be accounted for. Everyone needs a role. And that cellar... someone has been redecorating it. In an abandoned manor with no visitors since 1937. That's the piece that doesn't fit. That's the locked box I haven't opened yet.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, the ventilation system — just as I feared, I'm afraid. Quite corroded in places. Several of these vents seem to connect directly to the upper floors — the library and entrance hall, if I'm not mistaken. I shall have to make a note for the maintenance schedule. Terribly important, proper airflow — one wouldn't want any unpleasant surprises with the laboratory chemicals upstairs. Now then — I see we have quite the gathering down here! I do hope the Gruesome family has been making you feel welcome. I must say, I'm rather curious about these decorations. Someone has been busy. But I really ought to return to Miss Bellingham — as estate manager, I should be available to answer any questions about the manor. Shall we head back up?
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob. Again. A cold tightness wraps around my ribs like a band being screwed shut. They followed me to the cellar. They are shadowing me deliberately now — not even pretending it's about Miss Pitstop anymore, because she's not here. This is about me. My neck is hot and my stomach has dropped, that old familiar lurch — the boy with the sandwich, the moment you realize someone has seen through you before you were ready. No. No, they haven't seen through anything. They're suspicious, that's all. Suspicion is manageable. Suspicion is just a door that hasn't been opened yet, and I have the key to every door in this house. But I need to change tactics. I can't keep running room to room with the Mob on my heels — every move I make alone looks worse. I need to fold back into the group. Become invisible again. The best disguise isn't distance — it's proximity. Go back to Penelope. Be helpful. Be Pemberton. Be so utterly, tediously useful that the Mob's suspicion looks paranoid to everyone else. And Dastardly is here too — useful, greedy Dastardly. If I can get him alone, I can point him at something dangerous and let him take the consequences. But the vents — I learned something from interacting with them. I need to process that. And the furniture... someone has been down here. The cheerful decorations. That's a thread I haven't pulled yet. But the Mob is watching. Every second I linger here, their certainty grows. Back upstairs. Back to Pemberton. Back to the smile.

events.desc: The vents connect to the library and the entrance hall. That's the map I needed — the invisible architecture, the pathways no one sees. Laboratory fumes, properly directed, could fill either room. But the Ant Hill Mob is breathing down my neck, and every room I enter alone becomes a room they mark as suspicious. Time to change the game, Vincent. Stop running ahead. Fall in behind. Become the most helpful, most harmless, most boringly essential person in the manor. Let them watch Pemberton fuss over maintenance schedules and answer questions about Lord Doily's favourite curtains. And while they're watching the performance... the design completes itself in the dark.
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob. Again. A cold tightness wraps around my ribs like a band being screwed shut. They followed me to the cellar. They are shadowing me deliberately now — not even pretending it's about Miss Pitstop anymore, because she's not here. This is about me. My neck is hot and my stomach has dropped, that old familiar lurch — the boy with the sandwich, the moment you realize someone has seen through you before you were ready. No. No, they haven't seen through anything. They're suspicious, that's all. Suspicion is manageable. Suspicion is just a door that hasn't been opened yet, and I have the key to every door in this house. But I need to change tactics. I can't keep running room to room with the Mob on my heels — every move I make alone looks worse. I need to fold back into the group. Become invisible again. The best disguise isn't distance — it's proximity. Go back to Penelope. Be helpful. Be Pemberton. Be so utterly, tediously useful that the Mob's suspicion looks paranoid to everyone else. And Dastardly is here too — useful, greedy Dastardly. If I can get him alone, I can point him at something dangerous and let him take the consequences. But the vents — I learned something from interacting with them. I need to process that. And the furniture... someone has been down here. The cheerful decorations. That's a thread I haven't pulled yet. But the Mob is watching. Every second I linger here, their certainty grows. Back upstairs. Back to Pemberton. Back to the smile.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The tightness in my shoulders hasn't let go since I came down these stairs. It's worse now. This cellar — it's wrong. Everything about it is wrong. Damp stone walls, cobwebs, old furniture — that's what a cellar should be. But 'cheerful decorations'? Someone has been REDECORATING down here. Rearranging furniture with 'surprising care.' And air vents — a network of them — along the upper walls. Big enough for 'something very small to explore.' My skin crawls. This isn't a cellar that someone's been maintaining. This is a cellar that someone's been PREPARING. Like a room. Like a place you'd keep someone. The air vents — ventilation. You put ventilation in a room where someone needs to breathe. The furniture rearranged with care — making it comfortable. For who? For WHAT? And there's only one exit — back up to the laboratory. One way in, one way out. If someone got down here and the door closed... My gut goes cold. This is it. This is what Sneekly's been setting up. A room with one exit, cheerful enough to not immediately alarm, ventilated enough to keep someone alive, furnished enough to be comfortable. It's a TRAP. A gilded cage. For Clara. And I've walked right into it to find him. And Dastardly followed me down. And now Penelope's up there without me. STUPID, Danny! Your elaborate plan — come check the cellar, leave Peter with her — but now YOU'RE the one who's separated from her! You've done exactly what they wanted! But wait — wait. Give him the benefit of the doubt. Maybe... maybe the previous owner was eccentric. Maybe someone lived down here. Maybe the decorations are old. But the furniture's been rearranged RECENTLY. With care. By someone who's been here. Pemberton's been here. He manages the estate. He'd have access. Oh god. I need to look at this properly and then get back upstairs. Fast.

events.desc: I've been thick. Thick as two short planks. I came down 'ere to catch 'im at whatever 'e's doin', and instead I've left Penelope upstairs wivout me. That's what they wanted — split us up. Get the guard dog away from the girl. And I fell for it. But this cellar... this cellar tells me everyfink I need to know. Someone's been makin' it ready. Comfortable. Ventilated. One exit. It's a cage. A pretty cage, but a cage. I need to get back upstairs. NOW. Before they move 'er down 'ere.

events.thinking: A prickle across the back of my neck the moment I step down. The cellar is damp and cold but — cheerful decorations? Someone has been here. Recently. Carefully. And there's Pemberton, right where I expected him. My stomach does that tightening thing, the one where the count starts running. Pemberton. The Ant Hill Mob. Big Gruesome and Little Gruesome — enormous and tiny, like a cartoon. Red Max. This cellar is more crowded than the library was. So much for my private reconnaissance. But the furniture — rearranged with surprising care. That's not cobweb-and-neglect behaviour. That's someone building something. Preparing something. And the air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Something small like... Little Gruesome? Or Muttley? The vents connect rooms. They're a network. That's a back door into everywhere else in the manor. If I could get something — or someone — into those vents... But I have nothing. Empty hands. Empty pockets. My jaw tightens. I'm surrounded by people and I have nothing to trade, nothing to offer, nothing to scheme with. The Ant Hill Mob followed me down here specifically because they're suspicious of Pemberton — and of me. But the furniture. The old furniture, rearranged. There might be something hidden in it, under it, behind it. Something Pemberton was fussing with before we all arrived. That's where I should look. But I need to handle this carefully — the Mob are watching.

events.desc: Pemberton's been down here alone, 'checking the damp,' and the furniture has been moved with care. He knows something. Every room he enters, he leaves before everyone else arrives. Every room he leaves, he's already taken what he needs. The man is running the same playbook I am — arrive first, extract value, move on — except he does it quietly while I do it theatrically. I'd almost admire it if it weren't costing me the treasure. But I choose to believe the best in people. Perhaps he really is just a diligent estate manager with a passion for interior decorating. Perhaps. In the meantime, Reginald Foxworth will examine every stick of that carefully rearranged furniture.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
The hot weight behind my sternum has settled into my hands. They're steady now — engineer's hands, my father's hands. The machine is beautiful. Victorian brass-and-copper, three lever positions, a gauge that probably measures pressure or counterweight tension, and that gnawed wire. I can see exactly where it's severed — clean enough that my jaw tightens. Rats don't gnaw that neatly. But I said I'd give the benefit of the doubt. I said that.

She called me a wonder. She said 'that is exactly the kind of thinkin' that separates the engineers from the enthusiasts.' The coal in my chest is glowing now, warm and steady, like the bridge taking the weight. She sees it. She sees what I do.

But now — the Ant Hill Mob have gone to the cellar after Sneekly, and Dastardly has followed them down too, spouting about humidity preservation and monographs. It's just me, her, Rufus, and Sawtooth in this room. The Mob told me to stay with her. Don't let her out of my sight. That's not a hardship — that's exactly where James Hartwell wants to be.

The machine needs three operators. The wire needs fixing. The wrench is missing — she noticed that too, clever as always. The wrench is somewhere else in the manor, deliberately separated from the machine. That's Lord Doily's security system — you can't operate the machine without first finding the wrench to repair it, and you can't repair it without the wire, and you need three people coordinated. It's an elaborate lock.

But right now, with fewer people in the room, with her examining the workbench, with Rufus and Sawtooth nearby — this is my moment. Not to fix the machine yet, but to do something more important. She's right here. The Mob said stay with her. The others are gone. This is the quietest it's been since we arrived. I could — I could talk to her. Actually talk. Not declare, not narrate, not perform. Just... talk. The way Peter Perfect whispered to her. The way that made my chest hollow.

No. Not yet. The workbench first. She's examining it. I should be examining it with her. Looking for the brass disc. Working side by side. Like the school project. Like being eight years old and trying to impress her while she tried to make me laugh.

events.desc: She is three feet away, examining tools, and the light from the bubbling flasks is catching her hair, and James Hartwell is talking about spatial reasoning scores from school because James Hartwell has never once in his life known what to say to her that isn't about competence or engineering or load-bearing walls. Say something real, Hartwell. Say something that isn't a structural assessment. But the words that come are always the ones about what he can build. The other words — the ones about what he feels — they stick in his throat like they always have.
