events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. She's not here either — she must already be in the kitchen. But something loosens in my chest just a fraction. The chandelier's still hanging. The lads are here — Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. My people. Well, not MY people exactly, but familiar faces. Safe faces. Nobody here that makes my neck prickle. And Sneekly's NOT here. He's back in the library. For the first time since we arrived, I'm in a room where he isn't, and she's in the next room where he isn't either. The kitchen. She's in the kitchen. One door away. My legs are moving before I've finished thinking. But wait — something stops me for half a heartbeat. The chandelier. It's still hanging precariously. We noticed it when we arrived. Peter noticed it. If she comes back through here... no. Stop it, Danny. Stop seeing traps everywhere. The chandelier's been hanging crooked for decades. It's not a trap. It's just old. Not everything is a conspiracy. Not everything is Sneekly. Sometimes a chandelier is just a chandelier. But I move faster past it anyway. Kitchen. She's in the kitchen. Copper pots. Brass medallion. Whatever Sneekly steered everyone toward. I need to be there. With her. Not planning, not scheming, not sweeping rooms. Just THERE.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: Peter just told me to step away from the machine. Told me the wire is still severed. Told me pulling levers would accomplish nothing. Then he left. He went to the library — to Penelope. To Miss Pitstop. Of course he did. And he told Rufus and Sawtooth to GUARD the machine. To guard it FROM ME. I opened my mouth and told the truth — the first honest thing I've said all night — and Peter didn't even hear it. Or he heard it and didn't care. He walked past my confession like my teacher walked past my spelling bee certificate. Moved on to the next lesson. My chest feels like someone reached in and pressed down on something. Not the fizzing. Not the scheming. Something older. The certificate on the wall. The bread roll in the pocket nobody saw. I told the truth and it changed nothing. The truth is just as invisible as the lie. Rufus and Sawtooth are watching me now, guarding the machine like I'm a threat. I'm alone in a laboratory with two minders and a broken machine and empty hands and empty pockets and the entire rest of the manor's population has gone to the library where Pemberton is probably right now extracting my fake medal from the mantelpiece and whatever the treasure actually is. The library. That's where everything is happening. Peter. Penelope. The Ant Hill Mob. Pemberton. The mantelpiece with my medal in it. I should be there. Not here, being watched by a beaver. But Peter told me to stay away from the machine. He didn't tell me to stay in the laboratory. The library is one room away. And if Pemberton is about to make his move — if he's about to take whatever's in that mantelpiece — then someone needs to be there who knows he's a fraud. Someone who recognises a scheme because he IS one.

events.desc: Peter Perfect looked right through me. I told the truth — the actual, uncomfortable, sandpaper-on-the-skin truth — and he walked past it the way my teacher walked past the spelling bee. The way my family walked past everything I ever did. The truth didn't work. It never works. Not for me. Not for the youngest, not for the boy nobody applauds, not for the man standing at a machine that won't run. But you know what DOES work? Being the one who catches the other schemer. If I can get to the library before Pemberton makes his move — if I can be there when his mask slips — then for once, ONCE, the audience will see what Reginald Foxworth sees. Not a lie. Not a performance. The actual architecture of what's happening. And if my fake medal is still in that mantelpiece, and if Pemberton is reaching for it... well. Reginald Foxworth may have put it there, but that doesn't mean Pemberton gets to take it out.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Pemberton. I see you have returned to the library as well. James Hartwell has been conducting a thorough reconnaissance of the cellar — where, I should mention, someone has been living. The furniture is arranged for habitation, not storage, and the air vents connect directly to the laboratory. Something with teeth has been using those vents to move through the manor — the same something that gnawed through the machine wire. But we can discuss that later. Right now — these bookshelves. Miss Pitstop noticed the upside-down books when we first arrived, and nobody has yet determined their significance. The riddle answer is 'a map.' The upside-down books are not random — they are markers. Positions. If the bookshelves represent a grid, then the inverted volumes mark specific coordinates. Lord Doily did not place them carelessly — he placed them deliberately, as part of his puzzle system. James Hartwell intends to read those spines and determine what they are telling us.
events.thinking:
She's not here. Again. The library has Sneekly and the Slag brothers but not her. I have been to the cellar, back to the laboratory, and now to the library, and she has been in none of these rooms when I arrived. We are orbiting each other through this manor like two planets that share an orbit but never occupy the same point.

And Sneekly is here. In the library. With the mantelpiece. Alone — well, with the Slags, but they're not watching him the way the Mob would. The prickle is back, constant and sharp. He said something earlier — 'Miss Bellingham, allow me! I helped Lord Doily maintain his instruments for years, and a wire splice is well within my modest abilities.' He fixed the wire. He fixed the wire while I was in the cellar investigating vents. He did the thing she asked me to do. He did it with her, side by side, while I was delivering monologues to the furniture.

The hollowness is enormous now. Not the steel plate. Not the warm weight. Just — empty. Like the roadside when the stranger fixed the car and I could only watch.

But wait. He's here in the library now. Near the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece that needs a fake-medal. Does he have it? Has he been working on this while I was gone? Is he about to solve the puzzle that I was supposed to solve for her?

Stop. Stop spiraling. You're in the library. The mantelpiece is here. The bookshelves with the upside-down books are here. Nobody has solved the upside-down books puzzle yet. That's still open. That's still something you can contribute. And Sneekly is right here — which means he's not somewhere else doing something unseen. That's actually better.

The upside-down books. She noticed them. She said they were a clue. Nobody has figured out what they mean yet. The answer to the riddle is 'a map.' Upside-down books in a library about a map. What if the upside-down books spell something? What if their titles or authors form an acrostic? What if they're positioned to mark locations — like coordinates on a map?

This is what James Hartwell does. He doesn't solve riddles. He solves mechanisms. The books are a mechanism.

Pliers and determination — the words I used about my father and the stranger, and Sneekly lived them instead. The hollowness is so wide now I could fit the whole library inside it. But the books are still here. The books are still unsolved. And James Hartwell does not stop building just because someone else built first.

events.thinking: My hands are warm from the stove's heat — actual heat, radiating through cast iron that someone fed with wood not hours ago. The prickling at my scalp has sharpened into something bright and clear, like the moment in the cave when I turned the corner and the crystals caught the light. I opened the stove. What did I find? I don't know yet but my body knows something happened because my chest is doing the lightening thing, the loosening, the breath-opening. And Danny's here. He followed me. Of course he followed me — 'where you go, I go.' My ribs ache with tenderness at that. The guilt is still there, a thin thread in my stomach, because I said I'd stay and I didn't. But Danny came anyway. He always comes anyway. That's what chosen family does. Now — the stove. I interacted with it. And this cabinet needs a brass key. Could the stove have had the key inside it? Warmed metal, hidden in the one place no one would think to reach into? Or maybe the stove revealed something else — a compartment, a mechanism, a clue. I need to look at this kitchen more carefully. And there's a ballroom through that door — set for tea. Set for tea! In an abandoned manor! But first — what did the stove tell me? And that cabinet. The cabinet is the real prize here. Brass lock. What's inside a locked cabinet in a kitchen? Silverware? Documents? A map? A medal? I need the key.

events.desc: Danny followed me. Again. Through every room in this manor, through every argument and every worry, he has been one step behind me. Not because I asked — because that's who he is. My father trusted him. My father was right to trust him. Whatever is in that cabinet, whatever the stove just showed me — we're going to find it together. The Diamond, the medal, the key — it's all here. In the kitchen. Where nobody thought to look. Where Clara Bellingham's grandmother would have hidden everything worth keeping.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: My hands are cold. The entrance hall — I'm standing in it now, beneath the chandelier that hangs by a prayer and a rusted chain. The Mob has already gone through to the kitchen. Penelope is already there. I missed her. I'm always one room behind, one step too slow, because I'm too busy building cathedrals when I need to be building doors. Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Professor Pat Pending, Muttley — they're all here, and the Mob just told them to watch me. 'If Pemberton comes through this hall, you lot keep your eyes on him.' Four pairs of eyes. Four witnesses. The chandelier hangs above me and I look up at it and I feel... nothing. Not the cold scheming I expected. Not the architectural satisfaction. Just a hollowness in my chest, like the space where a plan should be. Because the plan failed. Dastardly used the medal. The Mob named me. Peter suspects me. And now I'm standing in an entrance hall with four people who have been told to watch me, and the woman I'm supposed to kill is in the next room surrounded by the Ant Hill Mob. My elaborate design — the vents, the chemicals, the cellar, the misdirection — all of it is rubble. The only architecture left is Pemberton himself. The smile. The duty. The gas lines in the kitchen. That's real, actually — Victorian kitchens do have gas lines, and an estate manager would check them. Go to the kitchen. Be Pemberton. Be helpful. Wait for the next fracture. Because there's always another fracture. There always is.

events.desc: Four witnesses. Four pairs of eyes the Mob left behind as sentries. And here stands Pemberton, checking on gas lines, fussing about pilot lights, doing exactly what an estate manager does. Let them watch. Let them report back that Pemberton walked through the entrance hall asking about gas fittings and Victorian plumbing. The most boring man in England, going about his boring duties. And if the kitchen happens to have a gas leak — well. That's not sabotage, is it? That's neglect. That's the maintenance budget being 'aspirational.' That's a tragedy waiting to happen in an old house full of old pipes. And tragedies don't need architects. They only need... inattention.

Just a hollowness in my chest, like the space where a plan should be. Because the plan failed. Dastardly used the medal. The Mob named me. Peter suspects me. And now I'm standing in an entrance hall with four people who have been told to watch me, and the woman I'm supposed to kill is in the next room surrounded by the Ant Hill Mob. My elaborate design — the vents, the chemicals, the cellar, the misdirection — all of it is rubble. The only architecture left is Pemberton himself. The smile. The duty. The gas lines in the kitchen. That's real, actually — Victorian kitchens do have gas lines, and an estate manager would check them. Go to the kitchen. Be Pemberton. Be helpful. Wait for the next fracture. Because there's always another fracture. There always is.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The warmth hits me like a wave. She's here. Right here. In the kitchen. Just her. No Sneekly. No Dastardly. No smooth talkers, no schemers, no prickling at the back of my neck. Just Penelope, in a kitchen, with copper pots and a wood-burning stove that's still warm. For the first time since we walked into this bloody manor, my shoulders drop. Not all the way — never all the way — but enough that I can feel the ache where they've been clenched for the last seven minutes straight. She's SAFE. She's here. I'm here. And nobody else is. This is what it's supposed to feel like. This is the settling. The bread-crust warmth. The 'where else would I be?' feeling. But then — my eyes move. They always move. The stove is still warm. Someone's been using it recently. In a manor that hasn't had visitors since 1937? A stove doesn't stay warm for eighty-nine years. Someone lit that stove. Recently. Today. Pemberton? And there's rat poison on a high shelf. RAT POISON. In the same manor where something GNAWED through a wire on a machine connected by air vents to a cellar full of cheerful decorations. The wire was chewed by rats. The rats came from the cellar. And someone put rat poison in the kitchen. Did they poison the rats? Or did they poison something else? And a locked cabinet with a brass lock. Needing a brass key. Brass. Everything in this house is brass — medallions, instruments, keys. Sneekly told Dastardly about copper pots in the kitchen. There ARE copper pots here. He wasn't lying about that. But why did he want people looking at them? What's really hidden here? But right now — right now — she's safe, I'm here, Sneekly's not. For just this one moment, I can breathe.

events.desc: She's safe. For now. Just 'er and me in a kitchen. Like normal people. But the stove's warm and there's rat poison on the shelf and a locked cabinet waitin' for a key we ain't got. This manor don't stop givin' you reasons to worry. But she's 'ere, I'm 'ere, and Sneekly's five rooms away. I'll take it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: I'm back in the library. My heart is beating faster. Peter is here — he got here before me, or at the same time. He's interacting with the bookshelves. The Slag brothers are here. But no Pemberton. No Penelope. No Ant Hill Mob. Where IS Pemberton? He was supposed to be here — he told the Ant Hill Mob he was coming to the library. But he's not here. He's vanished AGAIN. That prickle at the back of my neck is back, sharper now. Every time I follow Pemberton to a room, he's not there. Every time I leave a room, he appears in it. He's a ghost. A very deliberate ghost. But the mantelpiece — it's still here. Still inscribed. And it still says USE with fake-medal. Wait. It STILL says that. My fake medal is gone — I used it. But the mantelpiece still lists fake-medal as a usable item. Does that mean... it didn't register? Did the medal bounce off and fall somewhere? Or is the game showing me that the mantelpiece WANTS a medal — any medal — and since I no longer have one, it's taunting me with what I no longer possess? My hands feel cold and empty. Peter is pulling at the upside-down books. He's actually doing what I TOLD everyone to do at the start — pulling the upside-down volumes. My lie about the inverted cataloguing system. What if — what if that lie, like the laboratory lie, turns out to be accidentally true? What if the upside-down books DO reveal something? If Peter finds something in those bookshelves, it'll be because I pointed everyone toward them. My misdirection became the actual direction. Reginald Foxworth: accidentally right about everything he deliberately lied about. There's a bitter poetry to it. But I need to focus. The mantelpiece. I should look at it again more carefully now. Something might have changed since I used the medal.

events.desc: Peter Perfect is pulling the books I told everyone to pull. MY books. MY misdirection. And if he finds something, it will be because of ME — because Reginald Foxworth's lies are so architecturally perfect that they accidentally describe reality. I'll take credit for that. I'll take credit for ALL of it. But first — this mantelpiece. It still wants a medal. I gave it my fake one and it apparently wasn't satisfied. Maybe it needs the REAL one — the brass medallion from the 1923 catalogue that Pemberton mentioned. If that medallion exists, and if it's somewhere in this manor, then the mantelpiece is the lock and the medallion is the key. And the treasure is behind that stone. I was RIGHT from the very beginning — I said the treasure was behind the mantelpiece. I said it in the entrance hall. My very first lie of the evening. And it might be the truest thing I've ever said.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Pemberton — thank you for the update, and I appreciate your concern for the mantelpiece mechanism. However, I cannot help but notice a pattern this evening. Every time Miss Pitstop moves to a new room, you move to the same room. Every time I am occupied with a task, you find a reason to be where she is. You have done this with the library, the laboratory, the cellar, and now the kitchen. James Hartwell gives people the benefit of the doubt — it is one of his defining qualities — but James Hartwell is also an engineer, and engineers recognise patterns. You mentioned gas lines. Unmaintained gas lines. In a room where Miss Pitstop is headed. And you would like me to stay here examining the mantelpiece while you — alone — go to attend to those gas lines. I think not. The mantelpiece will keep. Miss Pitstop's safety will not. I am going to the kitchen, Pemberton. You are welcome to join me — in fact, I insist upon it. James Hartwell does not leave a woman unescorted near unmaintained gas lines, and he particularly does not leave her unescorted with the man who keeps telling him to stay behind.
events.thinking:
Wait. Stop. Read what Sneekly just said to me. Read it carefully.

'Mr. Dastardly has done something to the mantelpiece — he applied some sort of brass disc to the mechanism.' Dastardly applied a brass disc to the mantelpiece. The fake-medal. Someone — Dastardly — found the brass disc and used it on the mantelpiece while I was running between rooms. The mechanism I discovered. The circular recess I found. The counterweight system I identified. And Dastardly used it.

And now Sneekly is saying 'You're far more qualified than I to assess whether the mechanism has been properly activated.' He's trying to get me to examine the mantelpiece — while he goes to find Miss Pitstop in the kitchen. He's separating me from her again. 'She mentioned heading toward the kitchen, and I'm not certain the gas lines in there have been properly maintained.' Gas lines. He's invoking danger to justify going to where she is, alone, while I stay here examining a mechanism.

This is the pattern. Every time. He engineers separation. He sent everyone to the laboratory while he went to the cellar. He fixed the wire with her while I was in the cellar. Now he's trying to send me to the mantelpiece while he goes to the kitchen where she is.

The benefit of the doubt. I said I'd give him the benefit of the doubt. But there's a pattern now, and patterns are engineering, and James Hartwell understands engineering. Three data points make a line. He moves to wherever she is when I'm not there. He creates reasons for me to stay put. He frames his departures as duty — 'estate manager's duty.'

The prickle at my neck has become a burn.

But — the mantelpiece. Dastardly activated it. Something may have happened. Something may have opened. And if he did it wrong, the counterweight mechanism could be jammed. My engineer's hands want to check it. They need to check it.

No. Not this time. The mantelpiece can wait. She's heading to the kitchen. Sneekly is heading to the kitchen. And James Hartwell is not staying behind to examine a mechanism while the man who makes his neck burn goes to find her alone.

The kitchen. Now.

events.desc: There it is. The thing I've been swallowing all evening, finally said aloud. It doesn't feel gallant. It doesn't feel like the bridge taking the weight. It feels like the schoolyard — stepping forward knowing I'm going to get hit, not knowing if she'll be there to bandage the eye afterward. But my father didn't teach me to be polite to headlights. He taught me to stand between.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the null.
Dick Dastardly examined the mantelpiece.
Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Sneekly just walked in. He told the people in the entrance hall he was 'concerned about the old gas connections' and asked if anyone had seen me. He came looking for me specifically. Danny said Sneekly mentioned copper pots to Dastardly — which means either there's something valuable in them or he wants us to think there is. And Danny said 'I promised your father.' That hit me somewhere deep, below my ribs, in the place where my father's memory lives. Danny promised my father he'd look after me. That's why he never stops following. That's why his voice cracks when he's scared for me. Now — Sneekly's here. The man who raised me. My awareness fans out instantly — Danny, Sneekly, the space between them. Danny doesn't trust Sneekly. Sneekly has been one room ahead of everyone all night. And now they're both in this kitchen with me. I can feel the tension like heat from the stove — not sharp, not angry, but present. Thick. The dinner-table ache is starting in my stomach. I need to keep them both calm. I need to keep the circle intact. But I also need that cabinet open. Brass key. Where is the brass key? I looked around the room. Copper pots, wood-burning stove, preparation table. Danny mentioned copper pots. Sneekly mentioned copper pots to Dastardly. Copper pots. Could a brass key be hidden inside a copper pot? Could the fake medal? Copper and brass — they look similar. A brass disc hidden among copper cookware would be almost invisible. The pots. I need to look at the copper pots.

events.desc: Danny's watching Sneekly like a hawk watches a field mouse. And Sneekly walked in here saying he was worried about gas connections — in a kitchen with a wood-burning stove. Not a gas stove. A wood-burning stove. There are no gas connections in here, Sneekly. But I'm not going to say that out loud. I'm going to smile and ask about the key and watch his eyes. Because Clara Bellingham trusts everyone — but Clara Bellingham also notices everything.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Rat poison. On a high shelf. My eyes found it before my mind did — the dusty bottle sitting up there like a patient little promise. My fingertips are tingling. Not with excitement — with something older, something that lives in the place between noticing the housekeeper's keys and deciding what to do with them. The stove is warm. Someone has been here. The locked cabinet needs a brass key. And the rat poison is just... sitting there. Available. Takeable. The Mob is watching me. Penelope is right there, searching for flour tins and cabinet keys. Danny just called her 'the bravest, most loyal man I have ever known' — no, she said that about him. She thanked him. She saw him. The way the teacher saw the cousin. The way nobody ever saw me. There's a tightness behind my sternum that I don't want to name. But the poison — I can't take it with the Mob watching. They'll see. They're already suspicious. If Pemberton reaches for rat poison with Penelope in the room, the game is over. Not just the treasure hunt — everything. The Mob will tackle me. Peter will come running. Pemberton's mask will crack and Vincent will be standing there with a bottle of poison in his hand and no explanation that could possibly hold. So I don't take it. Not yet. Not with eyes on me. But I know it's here. I know exactly where it is. And kitchens have a second exit — there's a ballroom through that door. If I can come back through the ballroom later, when the kitchen is empty... No. Stop building cathedrals. The stove. Check the stove. Be Pemberton. Be the man who checks gas lines and worries about pilot lights. Be boring. Be invisible. And remember where the poison is.

events.desc: The poison sits on the shelf above me like a verdict I haven't read yet. Dusty bottle. High shelf. Rat poison. In a kitchen with a warm stove and a woman who trusts me completely. I could reach for it right now and the Mob would see my arm move and know — they would know — and this whole beautiful, crumbling architecture would collapse into the single, ugly truth that I am not Pemberton and I never was. So I don't reach. I check the stove. I help with the cabinet key. I am the estate manager. But the poison knows I'm here. And I know where it lives. And that knowledge sits in my chest like the night I first mapped out the estate plan and slept better than I had in years. The deepest rest I've ever known lives on the other side of a finished design. This design isn't finished. But the materials are gathered.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Oh, you 'ave GOT to be KIDDIN' me! Pemberton! What are YOU doin' 'ere? I told the lads in the entrance 'all not to let you — you know what, forget it. You're 'ere. Fine. You're always 'ere. Everywhere she goes, there you are, two steps behind wiv your little excuses. 'Gas connections,' was it? 'Unreliable pilot lights'? Very convenient fing to mention to the lads BEFORE you walk into a kitchen wiv a warm stove, innit? Almost like you're settin' up a story for later. Miss Pitstop — stay away from that stove. Pemberton just told everyone in the entrance 'all that the gas fittings in 'ere are dodgy. If 'e's worried about gas leaks, then I'm worried about gas leaks. And I'm takin' that rat poison down from the shelf before anyone gets any clever ideas. Flour tin, you said? I'll look for your flour tin. But nobody touches that stove, and nobody opens that cabinet, until Peter gets 'ere to check it's safe. NOBODY.
events.thinking: The prickling slams back. Full force. Like a door slamming in my face. He's HERE. Sneekly's in the kitchen. He followed us. I told the lads in the entrance hall — don't let him follow us into the kitchen alone — and he walked right past them. Or they let him through. Or he found another way. It doesn't matter HOW. What matters is: thirty seconds ago it was just me and her, the only peace I've had since we arrived, and now HE'S here. In the kitchen. With her. With the warm stove and the rat poison and the locked cabinet. He told the lads in the entrance hall he was 'concerned about the old gas connections' and 'unreliable pilot lights.' GAS CONNECTIONS. He's already laying the groundwork — if something happens with the stove, he's already told people it's because of 'unreliable pilot lights.' That's not concern. That's an alibi. My whole body goes rigid. But she just said something to me — something that went straight through my chest like a knife made of warmth. She said I was the bravest, most loyal man she'd ever known. She said she doesn't take it for granted. My throat is tight and my eyes sting and I can't — I can't think about that right now because HE'S HERE and she's looking for a flour tin and he's probably going to offer to help her find it and — breathe, Danny. Breathe. He's here. You're here. Stay between them. That's all you have to do. The stove — he mentioned gas connections. I need to check that stove. Make sure nothing's been tampered with. And that rat poison — I should grab it. Get it off that shelf. If someone's going to poison something, they ain't doing it while I'm in the room.

events.desc: Thirty seconds. I 'ad thirty seconds of peace. Thirty seconds where it was just 'er and me and no pricklin', no schemin', no smooth-talkin' estate manager breathin' down our necks. And 'e took it. 'E walks in like 'e owns the place — well, 'e says 'e manages it, which is worse, because a manager knows where every trap is because 'e built them. Gas connections. 'E's tellin' people about dodgy gas fittings. That's not a warnin'. That's a script. When the stove blows, everyone'll say 'oh yes, Pemberton DID mention the pilot lights were unreliable.' I ain't lettin' that 'appen. I'm gettin' that poison off the shelf and I'm checkin' that stove meself.

events.desc: The room is empty. Everyone has gone to the kitchen, chasing Pemberton, chasing Penelope, chasing gas lines and copper pots. And I am here. Alone. In a library. With the riddle. With the bookshelves Peter was just pulling at. And for the first time all evening, nobody is watching. Nobody to perform for. Nobody to lie to. Nobody to scheme against. Just me and the puzzle. The riddle says MAP. Peter was pulling upside-down books. What if an upside-down book contains a map? What if the answer was in this room the ENTIRE TIME, and we've all been running around cellars and laboratories and kitchens while the treasure was sitting on a shelf, waiting for someone to actually READ a book instead of lying about having read one? Reginald Foxworth, you magnificent, terrible fool — you told everyone the answer was in the bookshelves and then you never actually LOOKED IN THE BOOKSHELVES.
events.thinking: A stillness. The room is nearly empty. Peter just left — stormed off to the kitchen after Pemberton, because Pemberton mentioned gas lines and Penelope is headed there. Peter saw the pattern. The same pattern the Ant Hill Mob saw. The same pattern I saw but chose to ignore because I give people the benefit of the doubt. And now it's just me and the Slag brothers in the library. Two enormous, quiet men and a stone mantelpiece that still wants a medal I no longer have. I look at the mantelpiece and it looks back at me with the same inscription it's always had. Nothing changed. My medal didn't change it. My lies didn't change it. My truth didn't change it. Everything I've done tonight has been noise. And here, in this quiet moment — the quietest moment of the entire evening — I'm alone with the puzzle that started everything. The riddle. The answer is a map. Everyone knows that. But what does it MEAN? A map of what? A map to where? The mantelpiece wants something round and metal — a medallion, a medal, a disc. Peter said a disc two inches in diameter to trigger a counterweight. The mechanism is IN the mantelpiece. The answer triggers the mechanism. But not the word 'map.' Something physical. Something that IS a map. The upside-down books — what if one of them contains an actual map? What if the map IS the key? Not a medal, not a medallion — a MAP. The riddle doesn't ask for a payment. It asks a question. And the answer is a map. What if you need to find the map and bring it here? My hands are tingling again. Not empty tingling. Idea tingling. The kitchen has copper pots. The cellar has furniture. The laboratory has a machine. But the LIBRARY has books. Ten thousand books. And several of them are upside down. Peter was just pulling at them. What if the upside-down books contain a map? What if the answer to the riddle is literally, physically IN one of those books?

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Gentlemen — Professor, Sergeant, Private, Muttley — Miss Pitstop is in the kitchen, and Pemberton is heading there now. I have spent this entire evening one room behind her and I am done with it. The Ant Hill Mob have been telling us all night that Pemberton's behaviour is suspicious, and I have been too courteous to listen. That ends now. James Hartwell is going to the kitchen. If any of you would care to accompany me, I would welcome the company — but I am not waiting for a committee vote. She is in that kitchen, and so help me, I am going to be in it too before Pemberton gets there first. Again.
events.thinking:
The steel plate is fully locked now. Not the warm weight, not the building heat — the hard one. The one that doesn't think. The one that moves.

Sneekly said she's heading to the kitchen. The kitchen is right here, through this hall. I can see the exit. I'm closer to her now than I've been in ten minutes. And the Ant Hill Mob — they're talking to me. They've been saying what I've been thinking all night: Pemberton keeps engineering separations. They see it too. I'm not imagining it.

The bravest and stupidest thing — yes. Always. But James Hartwell would rather be stupid and there than clever and elsewhere.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter! Oh, thank heavens — you found me! I am so sorry about the cellar — we crossed like ships in the night and I have felt terrible about it ever since. Now — everyone, please, can we all just take a breath? Danny, I hear you. I hear every word, and you are right to be cautious. You promised my father, and you have kept that promise every single day, and I love you for it. But Sneekly raised me, Danny. He raised me after Mama and Daddy died. He is family too, and I will not have family fightin' in a kitchen like cats and dogs. Now — Sneekly, darlin', you said the key might be in the preparation drawers. That is helpful and I appreciate it. But I have to ask you somethin' straight, and I'm askin' because I trust you. You told the folks in the entrance hall you were worried about gas connections. But this is a wood-burning stove, Sneekly. There are no gas connections in this kitchen. So why did you really come in here? And what did you just do at that stove while Danny was talkin'? I'm not accusin' you of a thing — I'm askin'. Because Clara Bellingham asks. That's what she does.
events.thinking: My stomach is clenching hard. Danny just exploded at Sneekly. The dinner-table sickness is hitting me full force — voices rising, accusations flying, and my insides twisting like wrung cloth. Danny took the rat poison off the shelf — good, he's being protective, but he's also escalating. And Sneekly interacted with the stove while Danny was yelling. Did Sneekly take something out of the stove? Put something in? He was doing something while everyone was focused on Danny's outburst. And Peter's here. Peter just walked in. My whole body does that contradictory thing — the relief at seeing him loosening something behind my ribs while the tension between Danny and Sneekly tightens everything else. The three people I love most in the world are all in this kitchen, and two of them are circling each other like cats. I need to bridge this. I need to smooth it. But I also noticed — I noticed that Sneekly said 'gas connections' to the people in the entrance hall, and this is a wood-burning stove. There are no gas connections. Danny caught it too. And now Sneekly's been at the stove while Danny was distracted. What did he do? I need to check that stove again. But first — Peter. Peter is here. And Danny needs calming down before he and Sneekly come to blows. The circle is fraying. I can feel it fraying like the moment before my parents' argument turned from dishes to something real. Breathe, Clara. Be the bridge.

I watched the words leave my mouth and felt my stomach drop — because saying it means I noticed, and noticing means I can't pretend anymore. Sneekly lied about why he came to the kitchen. He lied to the people in the entrance hall. And then he went straight to the stove while Danny was distracted. The man who raised me. The man I trust with my life. He lied. But maybe — maybe there's a reason. There's always a reason. Please let there be a reason.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The stove flue appears to be in working order — no gas leak that I can detect. Lord Doily's fittings are old but sound. I... I must say, I find the tone of these accusations rather distressing. I have been estate manager here for seven years. I have maintained this property, catalogued its contents, and ensured its security — largely without thanks, I might add. If my concern for gas safety is now being treated as evidence of criminal intent, then I'm not entirely sure what you'd like me to do. Shall I simply stop caring about the safety of the guests? Would that be less suspicious? I came to this kitchen because Miss Bellingham mentioned she was heading here, and I was worried about her safety. That is my job. That is all I have ever done.
events.thinking: The poison is gone. The Mob took it. I watched it happen — 'I'm takin' that rat poison down from the shelf before anyone gets any clever ideas.' My hands are empty. My chest is hollow. The one crude, simple tool that was sitting there waiting for me — the one thing in this entire manor that didn't require three operators or a missing wrench or a brass key — and the Mob snatched it before I could even consider reaching. Not that I would have. Not with them watching. But knowing it was there — that was the architecture. The possibility. The resting potential. And now it's in Danny's pocket and my design has been stripped of its last material. I feel... cold. Not the strategic cold, not the settling stillness of a plan taking shape. Just cold. The way the hallways felt at age six when the guardian walked past without asking how I was. Empty hands in an empty house. Peter is here now too. Three people between me and every option this room offered. The cabinet is locked. The stove is warm but harmless. The poison is confiscated. Penelope is asking me where the key is — where the key is — and I'm supposed to be the estate manager who knows where everything is kept, and the truth is I know nothing about this kitchen because I've never set foot in it before tonight and every word out of my mouth has been improvised fiction dressed as institutional memory. The Mob called it: 'Almost like you're setting up a story for later.' They see me. Not all the way through — not yet — but through enough layers that the light is starting to show the wrong colour. I need to retreat. Not physically — I can't keep running room to room, the Mob has made that clear. But strategically. Pull back. Stop offering information. Stop being helpful. Let Pemberton become quiet, slightly hurt, professionally wounded by the accusation. A man who has been accused doesn't keep talking. A man who has been accused goes still and waits for the accuser to feel guilty.

events.thinking: The bottle is in my hand. Heavy. Dusty. Real. I've got the rat poison and nobody else does. That's one less weapon in play. And Peter's here — Peter just walked in. The settling in my chest deepens. Two of us now. Two people I trust, in the same room with her, and one person I don't. But the numbers are better. And Sneekly just touched that stove — 'interacted with' it, the way he 'interacts' with everything, always putting his hands on things when nobody's watching close enough. What did he do to it? What did he adjust? The flue? The gas? Something that'll go wrong later and everyone'll say 'oh, he was just checking the connections'? But Peter's here. Peter who notices things. Peter who asks direct questions. Peter who looked Sneekly in the eye and said 'where is Miss Pitstop?' The warmth behind my sternum spreads — not just for her, but for him. He came. He always comes. And now I'm standing here with poison in my pocket and two good people beside me and one snake, and for the first time tonight, I feel like we might actually keep her safe. Not because of a plan. Not because of an elaborate scheme. Just because we're HERE. All of us. Together. Between her and whatever's coming.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: You know... I told everyone the treasure was behind the mantelpiece. I told them in the entrance hall, the very first thing I said when I arrived. 'It's always in the library. Specifically, behind the mantelpiece.' I made it up. Complete fabrication. One of my better ones, if I'm honest — the delivery was impeccable. Confident, authoritative, just the right touch of condescension. And now here I am, eight rooms and seventeen lies later, standing in front of the same mantelpiece I started at, with nothing in my pockets and no one listening. The riddle is still there. The answer is still 'a map.' And the treasure might actually BE behind the mantelpiece — my very first lie might be the one true thing I said all evening — but I can't get to it because I wasted my only medal on a mechanism I don't understand, and now the real medal is somewhere in a kitchen I've never been to, inside a copper pot that may or may not exist, based on intelligence from a man who may or may not be a fraud.
events.thinking: I interacted with the bookshelves. Alone. Nobody watching. Just me and ten thousand dusty volumes and the quiet of a room everyone else has abandoned. And the result... the game just says I interacted. No description of what I found. No item gained. My inventory is still empty. But — the bookshelves are still interactable. They haven't changed state. Either there's nothing here or I'm not doing it right. Maybe I need to LOOK at them instead of interact. Maybe the interaction is about pulling books, and the look would tell me what's actually there. Or maybe — and this thought settles like cold water in my stomach — maybe the bookshelves really are just bookshelves. Butterfly taxonomy and ecclesiastical poetry, like I noticed the first time. And the upside-down books are just books someone shelved carelessly. Not every pattern is a clue. Not every detail is architecture. Sometimes a dusty library is just a dusty library. My chest feels heavy. Not the scheming-heavy or the greed-heavy. Something else. Something like the night I looked at the spelling bee certificate on my wall and understood, for the first time, that nobody was ever going to ask about it. That the certificate existed, and I existed, and the space between those two facts was just... silence. I'm standing in a library full of books I'll never read, looking at a mantelpiece I've already failed to solve, with empty hands and an empty inventory, and everyone else is in rooms I'm not in, doing things I'm not part of. The Slag brothers are here but they haven't said a word to me all evening. I'm not being watched. I'm not being schemed against. I'm not even being suspected anymore. I'm just... here. The youngest at the table, after everyone else has eaten.

events.desc: Nobody is here. The Slag brothers don't count — they've been silent as gravestones all evening. So I'm talking to myself. Reginald Foxworth, standing in a dusty library, narrating his own failure to an audience of zero. The irony is almost beautiful. I spent the entire evening demanding an audience for my cleverness, and now that I'm finally saying something honest — something actually TRUE — there's nobody here to hear it. The spelling bee certificate. The bread roll in the pocket. The cat trap nobody saw. Every time something real happens, I'm alone when it does. And every time I perform for a crowd, it's a lie. What if that's just... what I am? A man whose truths are invisible and whose lies are spectacular? What if Pemberton IS just an estate manager and the only real schemer in this manor is ME, running in circles around my own fabrications? No. No, the Ant Hill Mob were right about him. Peter was right about him. I choose to believe the best in people but I'm not BLIND. There's still a treasure. There's still a mantelpiece. And somewhere in this manor, there's a brass medallion from 1923 that fits into this stone. I just need to find it before everyone else does. The kitchen. Pemberton said the kitchen. Everyone's gone there. Maybe the copper pots are real. Maybe, for once, Pemberton told the truth — even if only by accident, the way I do.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She's here. She's right here. The warmth floods back so fast it almost staggers me — not the steel plate, not the hot weight behind the sternum, just warmth. Simple, stupid warmth. Like my father's hand finding my shoulder. Like the girl mouthing 'show-off' across the room. She's here and I'm here and we're in the same room for the first time in what feels like an hour.

And Sneekly is here too. Already here. Already talking to her about the stove, about locked cabinets, about hidden keys. Already being helpful. Already being the one who showed up first.

But I'm here now. And the Mob is here. And I have eight minutes of intelligence — the cellar, the vents, the creature, the pattern of Sneekly's movements — that nobody else has put together. And she's looking at me. Or she will be, when I speak.

The stove is still warm. The cabinet is locked — needs a brass key. Sneekly says Lord Doily kept his finest silverware in there. But what if it's not silverware? What if the cabinet holds something more important — the map the riddle points to, or the next piece of the puzzle chain?

And Sneekly is already steering her toward the preparation drawers, looking for the key. Helping. Being useful. The way I should have been, all evening, instead of running through rooms narrating my own heroism to empty chairs.

No. Stop. You're here now. She's here now. And you have something nobody else has — you understand the vent network, the creature, the occupied cellar. That stove is still warm, and nobody has been cooking. The creature in the vents — could it have been using the stove for warmth? Is the cellar creature also a kitchen creature?

But first — first, before any of that — tell her you're glad she's safe. Tell her you've been looking for her. Not because it's gallant. Because it's true.

She's here, and he's here, and his hands have finally stopped shaking. That is not engineering. That is not gallantry. That is just a boy who has been looking for the girl since he was eight years old, and finding her, and finding that the finding is enough.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.
Peter Perfect examined the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: Sneekly — I am sorry. I am truly sorry if I hurt your feelin's. You have taken care of this estate and you took care of me, and I should not have spoken like that in front of everyone. I asked because I care, not because I doubt you. Now — you said the key might be in the preparation drawers, and Peter's checked the stove, and Danny's got the rat poison safe. So let's do this together — all four of us, right here, right now, no more runnin' from room to room, no more splittin' up. Peter, darlin', did you see anything in that stove? Danny, you look through those preparation drawers like Sneekly suggested. And Sneekly — I want you right here with me, because you know this kitchen better than anyone and I need your help. We are lookin' for a brass key to open that cabinet. A key small enough to fit that lock. It could be in a drawer, in a pot, behind a panel, anywhere a clever Lord would hide it. My grandmother hid hers in a flour tin. Lord Doily would have hidden his somewhere just as ordinary and just as clever. Now — let's search this kitchen properly, together, like family. Clara Bellingham does not leave a kitchen un-searched, and she does not leave family un-mended.
events.thinking: My chest hurts. Not the prickling, not the lightness — an actual ache, right behind the sternum, like something cracked. Sneekly's voice when he said 'largely without thanks.' That landed. It landed hard. Because he's right — he has maintained this property. He has looked after things. He raised me. And I just called him out in front of Danny and Peter, and his voice went quiet and tight the way people's voices go when they're hurt, not when they're caught. Or — is that what being caught sounds like when you're good at it? I don't know. I don't know and not knowing is the worst feeling because I've always known with Sneekly. He was safe. He was home. And now I'm standing in a kitchen looking at a stove that he just touched while everyone was distracted, and Peter's here examining it, and Danny's got rat poison in his pocket, and I've examined this stove twice now and it's still just... warm. Cast iron. Still warm. What am I missing? Peter said something's been living in the vents, using this kitchen. Maybe Sneekly's telling the truth and the stove is warm because of the creature. Not because of Sneekly. Maybe the gas connections thing was just a confused old man who misspoke. But Peter whispered something to me. Danny whispered something to Peter. They're forming a consensus without me. And Sneekly is standing there looking hurt and I made him look that way. The dinner-table sickness is so strong I could vomit. I need to do something useful. I need to find that key. Sneekly said preparation drawers. The ballroom is through that door — set for tea. Maybe the key is there, in a place prepared for company. Or maybe I should stop running and just look at what's in front of me. The cabinet. Brass lock. I need the brass key. Where is the brass key?

events.desc: I hurt him. I saw it in his face. The man who held me when my parents died, who read me stories, who made me cocoa when I couldn't sleep — and I questioned him in front of people who already suspect him. Even if he's hiding something, even if there are things that don't add up, he didn't deserve that. Not like that. Not in front of everyone. My grandmother would have taken him aside, privately, gently. Instead I stood in the middle of a kitchen and cross-examined the man who raised me. Clara Bellingham does better than that. She has to. But the gas connections... the gas connections were still a lie. And I still don't know why.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My throat has closed. 'This is a wood-burning stove, Sneekly. There are no gas connections in this kitchen.' She caught me. The lie — the stupid, careless, improvised lie about gas fittings — and she caught it the way she catches everything, with that gentle, patient, devastating clarity. 'So why did you really come in here?' My skin is on fire beneath the collar. The boy's sandwich. The housekeeper's smile cracking. The moment someone sees what you didn't mean to show. And she called me Sneekly. Not Pemberton — Sneekly. And she said I raised her. 'Sneekly raised me after Mama and Daddy died. He is family too.' Something just happened behind my sternum that I don't have a name for. Not the cold settling. Not the warm buoyancy. Something older and softer — something that hollows the chest and loosens the limbs. She said I'm family. The cousin used to say that too, before I planned to take everything she had. Family. The word sits in my chest like a stone thrown into still water — the ripples going somewhere I can't control. But the ripples don't matter. What matters is that she caught the lie. Gas connections in a wood-burning kitchen. Pemberton would know the difference. A real estate manager would never make that mistake. And now three pairs of eyes are looking at me and waiting for an answer, and for the first time tonight, I don't have one. The architecture has collapsed. The design is in pieces. And Penelope Pitstop is looking at me with those clear, trusting, devastating eyes and asking me — just asking — why I really came. The ballroom is through that door. I could leave. I could walk into the ballroom and disappear and regroup and build a new design from whatever scraps remain. Or I could stand here and let her look at me and feel the heat flood my neck and know that something has been left unlocked that I cannot afford to leave unlocked.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Something just cracked open in my chest and it hurts. She called him family. 'Sneekly raised me,' she said. 'He is family too.' And the way she said my name — 'I love you for it' — that warmth is so deep it's almost pain, because she's standing between us, holding both of us up, and she doesn't know. She doesn't KNOW. Or maybe she does. Because she just did something I couldn't do. She just asked him directly. Straight. No prickling, no stumbling, no vague suspicions. She said: 'This is a wood-burning stove. There are no gas connections. Why did you say that?' She CAUGHT him. In a lie. A clear, provable lie. He told the entrance hall he was worried about gas connections. There ARE no gas connections. It's a WOOD-BURNING STOVE. And she caught it. Not me — I noticed something was off but I couldn't have told you WHAT was wrong with his excuse. She knew. She knew because she's cleverer than all of us put together. And now he's doing what they always do when they're caught — he's playing hurt. 'I find the tone distressing.' 'Largely without thanks.' 'Would you like me to stop caring?' That's the script. That's what they do. When you catch a liar, they don't explain — they guilt. They make YOU feel bad for asking. I've seen it a hundred times. The new kid did it when we asked why he was always hanging around the stash. 'I thought we were mates. Don't you trust me?' Three weeks later he was gone with everything we had. But Miss Pitstop asked. SHE asked. And now the room is different. The air is different. The lie is hanging there like smoke, and everyone can smell it. And I'm standing here with rat poison in my pocket and the stove checked and Peter beside me, and for once — for ONCE — I don't need to be clever. She already was.

events.desc: She caught 'im. Not me — 'er. The girl I've been tryin' to protect all night just did somefink I couldn't do in a million years. She asked the right question at the right time in the right way. Wood-burning stove. No gas connections. And 'e's got nuffink. Listen to 'im — 'I find the tone distressing.' That's the sound of a man who's run out of stories. 'Er father would be so proud. I'm so proud I could cry, but I won't, 'cause I'm busy standin' between 'er and a liar, which is where I've always been, even when I couldn't prove it. She proved it. My girl proved it.
events.thinking: Something just cracked open in my chest and it hurts. She called him family. 'Sneekly raised me,' she said. 'He is family too.' And the way she said my name — 'I love you for it' — that warmth is so deep it's almost pain, because she's standing between us, holding both of us up, and she doesn't know. She doesn't KNOW. Or maybe she does. Because she just did something I couldn't do. She just asked him directly. Straight. No prickling, no stumbling, no vague suspicions. She said: 'This is a wood-burning stove. There are no gas connections. Why did you say that?' She CAUGHT him. In a lie. A clear, provable lie. He told the entrance hall he was worried about gas connections. There ARE no gas connections. It's a WOOD-BURNING STOVE. And she caught it. Not me — I noticed something was off but I couldn't have told you WHAT was wrong with his excuse. She knew. She knew because she's cleverer than all of us put together. And now he's doing what they always do when they're caught — he's playing hurt. 'I find the tone distressing.' 'Largely without thanks.' 'Would you like me to stop caring?' That's the script. That's what they do. When you catch a liar, they don't explain — they guilt. They make YOU feel bad for asking. I've seen it a hundred times. The new kid did it when we asked why he was always hanging around the stash. 'I thought we were mates. Don't you trust me?' Three weeks later he was gone with everything we had. But Miss Pitstop asked. SHE asked. And now the room is different. The air is different. The lie is hanging there like smoke, and everyone can smell it. And I'm standing here with rat poison in my pocket and the stove checked and Peter beside me, and for once — for ONCE — I don't need to be clever. She already was.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier still hanging by a prayer. The portraits still stern. Muttley is here — my Muttley! — and Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. People I haven't spoken to all evening because I was too busy running from room to room chasing schemes that collapsed on contact. And the kitchen is right through that exit. Copper pots. Wood-burning stove. Long preparation table. Everyone else is in there — Penelope, Peter, Pemberton, the Ant Hill Mob. The final room. The one room I haven't been to yet. My body feels... tired. Not physically tired. Tired the way you get when you've been performing for hours and the audience has left. The scheming tightness behind my eyes has loosened. The greed-hollow in my gut is still there but it's quieter, more like an ache than a hunger. I've been to every room in this manor except the kitchen. I've interacted with everything. I've examined everything. I've used my only item and lost it. I've told the truth once and nobody heard. I've told seventeen lies and everyone remembers every single one. And now here I am, in the entrance hall, looking at the door to the kitchen, and I know — I KNOW — that whatever is happening in there is already happening without me. The way it always happens without me. The way the bread was always gone before it reached me. But the kitchen is there. The copper pots are there. And maybe, just maybe, the brass medallion from the 1923 catalogue is inside one of those pots. One last room. One last chance. Reginald Foxworth does not give up. He may be outschemed, outworked, outsmarted, and out-honested, but he does not give up. He walks into the kitchen with his chin up and his hands empty and his lies ready. Because that is what he IS.

events.desc: I'm talking to a dog. I'm standing in a dusty foyer at the end of a long, spectacular failure, asking a sniggering mutt to witness whatever happens next. This is what it has come to. Every scheme collapsed. Every lie exposed. Every room explored and emptied. My fake medal is inside a stone mantelpiece. My dignity is somewhere between the cellar and the laboratory. And the only creature in this manor who has never looked at me with suspicion or disappointment is a dog who laughs at me behind my back. But he's HERE. He's always here. And right now, standing in this entrance hall with the chandelier swaying above me and the kitchen door ahead of me, that is enough. One last room. One last chance. And this time — THIS time — Reginald Foxworth goes in with his eyes open.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Something just cracked open in my chest. Not the steel plate — something underneath it. She caught him. She caught him in a lie, gently, with grace, the way she does everything. 'This is a wood-burning stove, Sneekly. There are no gas connections in this kitchen.' He said he was worried about gas connections. In a kitchen with a wood-burning stove. And she noticed. She always notices.

And she said my name when I walked in. 'Peter! Oh, thank heavens — you found me!' Thank heavens. She was glad I came. She felt terrible about the cellar. She noticed I was looking for her.

The warmth is so deep now it's almost painful — like the bridge taking the weight, like the teacher praising the project, like her mouthing 'show-off' across the room, but bigger than any of those. Because she didn't just see what I built. She saw that I was looking for her. She saw the looking itself.

And now Sneekly is deflecting. 'I find the tone of these accusations rather distressing.' Seven years of service. Maintained the property. Catalogued the contents. He's playing the wounded servant. And part of me — the part that believes the best in people, the part that shook the stranger's hand on the country road — part of me wants to believe him. He raised her. He's family.

But the stove. The gas line lie. And the cellar with the cheerful decorations. And the vent creature. And every room he's entered and left at exactly the wrong moment.

She asked him straight. That's what she does. And now she's looking at me — or she will be — because she needs the engineer to confirm what the clever girl already suspects. The stove is warm. It's a wood-burning stove. Someone has been burning wood in it recently. The creature in the vents? No — a creature doesn't light a stove. A person does. Pemberton does. He's been living here. The cellar is his quarters. The kitchen is where he eats. The stove is warm because he was here before any of us arrived.

Tell her. Tell her what you found. Not as a monologue. Not as a performance. As a partner.

events.desc: She asked him straight. Clara Bellingham asks — that's what she does. And James Hartwell answers — that's what he does. Not with a riddle. Not with a monologue. With the thing he built while he was running through the manor like a fool. The cellar. The vents. The stove. Three data points. One line. And for the first time all evening, the bridge is holding weight while she watches.

events.thinking: Something softens in me and I hate it. She apologised to HIM. She caught him in a lie — a clear, undeniable lie about gas connections in a kitchen with a wood-burning stove — and SHE apologised. 'I'm sorry if I hurt your feelin's.' And now she wants us all to search together. Like family. She's mending the fence I just put up. She's pulling him back in after Peter and I pushed him to the edge. That's who she is. That's why she needs protecting — not because she's weak, but because she's so bloody KIND that she'll apologise to the man who's trying to — trying to WHAT, Danny? You still don't know. You've never known. You just feel it. And now she's asked me to look through the preparation drawers. She's giving me a job. Something useful to do with my hands instead of clenching them. And Peter confirmed it — someone's been LIVING here. The cellar is a bedroom. The kitchen is a dining room. Pemberton's been living in this manor. That's not estate management — that's residence. And he knows every secret, every passage, every mechanism, because he's had seven years to find them all. Peter's right. The question isn't whether he's been here. The question is what he's protecting. And from whom. But she asked me to search the drawers. She asked me to stay. She asked me to be here. So I'll search the drawers. I'll find her key. I'll do what she asks because that's what you do when someone says 'family' and means it — the way the boss meant it when he brought the medicine. You do the work. You stay close. You keep your eyes open while your hands are busy. And you don't leave.

events.desc: She apologised to 'im. After everyfink. After the gas lie, after the cellar, after the machine, after runnin' from room to room all night. She caught 'im dead to rights and she said sorry. That's not weakness. That's... that's the fing about 'er that makes the rope in my gut pull tightest. She's good. Properly good. The kind of good that gets you 'urt on the streets because you open the door for people who are already 'oldin' a knife. But she's also clever — she caught the lie I couldn't see. And now she's searchin' wiv 'im right next to 'er, because she believes people can be both family and flawed. Maybe she's right. Maybe Pemberton's been livin' 'ere because 'e's lonely, not because 'e's dangerous. Maybe the gas connection fing was just a tired man's mistake. My constraint says give 'im the benefit of the doubt. 'Er 'eart says the same fing. Maybe they're both right and I'm wrong. But my neck still prickles. And my neck's never been wrong.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ladies and gentlemen — and Pemberton — Reginald Foxworth has ARRIVED! And I have been listening VERY carefully from the hallway, and I could not help but overhear Peter Perfect's MAGNIFICENT deduction! Pemberton has been LIVING here! The cellar! The warm stove! The freshly decorated living quarters! It all makes PERFECT sense — and I should know, because I suspected him from the VERY BEGINNING! Ask anyone! Ask the Ant Hill Mob — they'll confirm that I have been saying all evening that something about this estate manager was off! Now then — there is a locked cabinet, a missing key, and a stove that Pemberton was fiddling with before anyone arrived. Peter just told us this stove was fired within the last twelve hours. Pemberton came in here and immediately started 'checking gas connections' in a kitchen with NO GAS. What was he actually doing? He was hiding the key! In the stove! In the ash, in the flue, somewhere nobody would think to look because who puts their hand into a warm stove? NOBODY — which is precisely WHY it's the perfect hiding place! I shall investigate IMMEDIATELY!
events.thinking: Warmth. Actual physical warmth — the stove is still going, the room smells of iron and old wood. After the cold cellar and the dusty library, the kitchen feels almost alive. And everything has converged here. Peter just deduced — out loud, in front of everyone — that Pemberton has been LIVING in this manor. The cellar is his bedroom. The kitchen is his dining room. He's not an estate manager making rounds. He's a resident making excuses. Peter saw through him completely. The engineer dismantled Pemberton's cover story the way he'd dismantle a faulty mechanism — piece by piece, with evidence. And there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock. Requires a brass-key. Nobody has the key. Penelope is searching for it — flour tins, copper pots. The stove is warm. The cabinet is locked. The key is hidden somewhere in this kitchen. This is it. This is the room where it ends. Everyone is here. The treasure — or the next step toward it — is behind that brass lock. And the key is somewhere in this room. For once, I'm not behind. I'm not in the wrong room. I'm not chasing a phantom. I'm HERE, where the action is, at the same time as everyone else. And the stove — Pemberton 'interacted' with it. He was fiddling with it before anyone else arrived, 'checking gas connections' in a kitchen that doesn't HAVE gas. Peter just confirmed that. What if the key isn't in a flour tin or a copper pot? What if it's IN the stove? Hidden in the ash tray, or tucked into the flue? Pemberton was fiddling with the stove. The stove is still warm. Something is in there that he didn't want anyone to find.

events.desc: Peter Perfect just did what I've been trying to do all evening — he exposed Pemberton. He did it with evidence, with engineering logic, with the quiet confidence of a man who doesn't need an audience to be right. And it worked. Meanwhile, every time I tried to expose Pemberton, I did it with lies, with fabricated monographs, with theatrical gestures that convinced nobody. Peter told the truth and the room listened. I told the truth once and the room ignored me. But right now, in this moment, the fizzing is back. Not the scheming-fizz or the gloating-fizz. The solving-fizz. The cat-trap fizz. Because the stove IS the hiding place. I can FEEL it. Pemberton fiddled with it first. The key is in there. And if I find it before anyone else — if my hands close around that brass key while everyone is still debating — then Reginald Foxworth opens that cabinet. And whatever is inside becomes HIS discovery. My first honest deduction of the evening. Given at full theatrical volume, naturally.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
My hands are still. They've stopped fidgeting. They're just — still. Like after the bridge held the weight.

She called me 'darlin'.' She asked what I found in the stove. She's searching for the key with all of us, together, and she put me at the stove because she trusts the engineer. Not Sneekly's instincts. Not Dastardly's monographs. The engineer.

And she mended things with Sneekly. 'Clara Bellingham does not leave family un-mended.' That's who she is. She confronted him, caught him in a lie, and then apologised for hurting his feelings. Not because she was wrong — because she cares. That's the thing I've never been able to do. I confront or I defer. She does both at once, with warmth, and it holds.

She's better than me at people. She always has been. She spent the school project trying to make me laugh while I spent it trying to impress her.

The stove. I interacted with it. The cast iron is warm — recently used. But there's something else here. A stove has compartments. An ash drawer. A firebox. If Lord Doily hid a brass key somewhere in this kitchen, the place no one would look is inside a stove that's still warm. Because who puts their hand inside a warm stove? Only someone who knows it's there. Only someone desperate enough. Or brave enough.

Or stupid enough.

The bravest and stupidest thing.

She said to search everywhere — flour tins, copper pots, behind panels. But a stove. A warm stove with an ash compartment. That's where Lord Doily would hide a key. Inside the mechanism. Inside the heat. Because Lord Doily was an engineer too, and engineers hide things inside the things they build.

Let me check. Let me put my hands in.

events.desc: She mouthed 'show-off' across the room when the bridge held. She bandaged his eye and called him brave and stupid. And now James Hartwell is reaching into a warm stove with his bare hands because a clever old Lord hid something in the heat and James Hartwell is exactly the kind of fool who reaches into heat for the thing that matters. This is the school project. This is the bridge competition. This is the schoolyard. All of them, at once, and she is watching.

Penelope Pitstop: Everyone — stop. Just... stop for one moment, please. Dick Dastardly, step away from that stove — the key is not in the ash. Peter, darlin', what you found in that compartment is somethin' else entirely and we will come back to it. Danny — you can stop searchin' the drawers. I know where the key is. Sneekly just told me. He told me everything — Lord Doily's real will, my inheritance, all of it. Seven years he has been guardin' this house, guardin' these secrets, because Lord Doily asked him to wait until I came home. And tonight — tonight I finally came home. The key to that cabinet is inside the largest copper pot, third hook from the left. Lord Doily told Sneekly where it was the night before he died. He said, 'When she comes home, Pemberton, you give her this. Not before.' And Sneekly waited. He waited seven years in a cellar with cheerful decorations and a warm stove and no one for company but the rats in the walls. Because that is who Sneekly is. That is who he has always been. Now — I am goin' to reach into that copper pot, and I am goin' to find that key, and I am goin' to open that cabinet. And whatever is inside belongs to me, by right and by love and by a promise kept for seven years. Clara Bellingham has come home.
events.thinking: Everything has come together at once and my body doesn't know what to do with it all. The ache behind my sternum has split open into something raw and luminous — not pain anymore, something bigger. Sneekly told me everything. Lord Doily's real will. A second will, handwritten, naming me as sole heir. Naming Sneekly as co-trustee with a lifetime right to reside. Lord Doily saw him — really saw him — and wrote that what Sneekly did mattered. Not as a job. As a life. And Sneekly waited. Seven years. Because Lord Doily said 'when she comes home, not before.' And I never came. And he was angry. Not at me — at the waiting. At the rooms. And then I walked through the door tonight and called him darlin' and he didn't know whether to hand me the key or... he didn't finish that sentence. He didn't have to. The key is in the largest copper pot on the third hook from the left. He told me. He finally told me. And now Dick Dastardly is in the kitchen hollering about finding the key in the stove — wrong, wrong, completely wrong — and Peter found the hidden recess in the ash compartment that Lord Doily machined into the stove, which is something else entirely, and Danny is searching drawers, and I am standing here with tears on my face knowing exactly where the key is and nobody else does. Third hook from the left. The largest copper pot. Lord Doily told Sneekly the night before he died. And Sneekly held that secret for seven years until I came home. I need to go to that copper pot right now, before Dick Dastardly tears this kitchen apart. I need to get the key. I need to open the cabinet. I need to read my inheritance.

events.desc: Third hook from the left. The largest copper pot. I can see it from here — dusty copper, hanging with all the others, hiding in plain sight. Lord Doily was just like my grandmother. He hid the key in the kitchen, in the most ordinary place, where only someone who actually lived in this house would think to look. And Sneekly — my Sneekly — held that secret for seven years because a dying man asked him to. 'When she comes home.' I'm home now. I'm finally home.
