events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something is breaking apart inside me and I can feel every crack. She said 'Clara Bellingham is home now, and she is not leaving her family again.' Family. Again. The word keeps hitting the same place behind my sternum — the place where the wall is thickest, the place I calcified at age six when the guardian walked past without asking how I felt. And each time she says it, the wall doesn't crack — it softens. Like stone becoming chalk. Like something that was load-bearing turning out to be hollow. I told her about the will. I told her about the copper pot. I told her about Lord Doily writing that I deserved something. And I told it in a voice I've never heard myself use — not Pemberton's obsequious warble, not Vincent's grand theatre, but something underneath both of them. Something small and tired and true. And she didn't flinch. She didn't scan for the cost. She cried. She said she was sorry. She said she should have come sooner. Nobody has ever been sorry for me. Not once. Not ever. The boy with the sandwich wanted homework. The guardian fed me by obligation. The housekeeper complied because I found her key. But Clara is standing here being sorry because she thinks I was lonely, and the terrible thing is — she's right. I was lonely. Seven years in a cellar with cheerful decorations and the rooms echoing above me and the only warmth in the house coming from a stove I lit for myself every morning. And I told myself it was the plan. It was always the plan. But the plan is in pieces on the kitchen floor and Dastardly is digging through the stove ash and Peter is examining the hidden compartment and the key is in the copper pot — the third hook from the left — and she's going to find the will and read Lord Doily's words and know that she was always the heir and I was always the keeper and none of it — none of the scheming, the vents, the poison, the medallion — none of it was necessary. It was never necessary. The rooms were always going to be hers. And they were always going to be mine too. Lord Doily made sure of that. I just couldn't believe it. I couldn't believe that something was given without a price attached. So I spent seven years turning a gift into a scheme because schemes are the only architecture I trust. And now a woman I was supposed to kill is holding my hand and calling me family and I don't know how to stop the stone from becoming chalk.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: I... I got it wrong. Didn't I. All night. Runnin' from room to room, chasin' shadows, seein' traps in every corner. And 'e was just... 'e was just keepin' the lights on. Waitin'. Like I waited outside that door when I was eight years old. 'Cause leavin' felt like somefink breakin'. I know what that feels like, Pemberton. I do. I didn't WANT to know, but I do. Miss Pitstop — the key's in the copper pot. Third 'ook from the left. 'E told you where it is. A man 'oo wants to 'urt you don't tell you where the key is. 'E just... 'e just wanted you to come 'ome. And when you did, 'e couldn't... 'e couldn't get the words out fast enough 'cause people like me kept gettin' in the way. I'm sorry, Pemberton. I'm sorry I made this 'arder than it needed to be. I was wrong. My gut was... my gut read the shape right but the reason wrong. You wasn't settin' traps. You was settin' the table. For 'er. Peter — go wiv Miss Pitstop to check that copper pot. I'll stay 'ere. I'll... I'll stay 'ere.
events.thinking: Everything is shifting under my feet. The ground I've been standing on all night — the certainty that Pemberton was the threat, that he was scheming, that every move was calculated to harm her — it's cracking. Not breaking. Cracking. Because what he just said... seven years. He waited seven years. In a cellar. Keeping the lights on. Because Lord Doily said 'when she comes home.' And she never came. And he was angry — not at her, at the waiting. At the rooms. At being given acknowledgement and then having it locked inside a cabinet he couldn't open. That's... that's the boss. That's the boss bringing medicine. That's the older kid sharing food when he didn't have to. Pemberton stayed because someone saw him — really SAW him — and told him he mattered. And then that person died and left him alone with a promise and a locked cabinet and no one coming home. My throat is so tight I can barely swallow. Because I KNOW that feeling. I know what it is to sit outside a door all night because leaving feels like something breaking inside you. I know what it is to wait for someone who doesn't know you're waiting. And I know — God help me, I KNOW — that my neck has been prickling all night because Pemberton's behavior looked exactly like a man running a con. Moving from room to room. Always one step ahead. Excuses for everything. But it also looks exactly like a man who's been alone for seven years, trying to manage the one night that matters, the night she finally came home, and watching it spiral out of his control because people like Dastardly and people like ME kept getting in the way. The gas connection lie — that was panic. Not planning. Peter said so. The stove wasn't tampered with. The flue is sound. He didn't sabotage anything. He just... lied badly because he was scared we'd find out he lived here before he could tell her himself. And she already knows. She already forgave him. And now she's asking to talk to him alone in the ballroom and every fiber of my body wants to say no — NO, you do NOT go into a room alone with him — but she's not a child. She caught the gas lie. She asked the right questions. She's cleverer than me and kinder than me and she's standing there looking at him with eyes that see a man who waited seven years, not a man with a plan. Maybe she's right. Maybe my neck was wrong this time. Or maybe my neck was right about the shape of what it saw — the sneaking, the lies, the room-by-room movement — but wrong about the reason. He wasn't setting traps. He was setting the stage. For her. For tonight. For the moment he'd been waiting for since Lord Doily died. The copper pot. Third hook from the left. He told her where the key is. He TOLD her. A man with something to hide doesn't tell you where the key is. Unless he's been dying to tell you for seven years and he just couldn't find the words until someone asked.

events.desc: I was wrong. The prickling was real — it's always real — but this time it was readin' the wrong story into the right shapes. 'E moved from room to room because 'e was nervous. 'E lied about the gas because 'e panicked. 'E prepared the cellar because 'e LIVED there. 'E followed 'er because 'e's been waitin' seven years to give 'er what Lord Doily left. And I stood between 'em the whole time, the wall that nobody needed, blockin' a door that was never gonna 'urt 'er. 'Er father would've seen it. 'Er father always saw the best in people. I only ever learned to see the worst. Maybe that's why 'e trusted me to protect 'er — because someone 'oo only sees danger never lets it through. But tonight... tonight the danger wasn't real. And the man I was guardin' 'er from was the one person in this 'ouse who loved 'er almost as much as I do.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The stove is a dead end — I've checked it thoroughly and the key is NOT in there! But LISTEN — there's a BALLROOM through that door, and Pemberton — our friend the secret resident — has set a dining table for TEA in there! A tea service! In an abandoned ballroom! The same man who decorated the cellar, cooked on this stove, and has been living in this manor like a particularly well-dressed squatter! If Lord Doily never did anything merely for decoration — and PEMBERTON told us that himself — then that tea service isn't decoration either! The key is on that table! Under a cup! Inside a teapot! Embedded in a scone, for all I know! Pemberton has been hiding things in plain sight all evening — furniture that's been moved, stoves that are warm, decorations that appeared overnight! The ballroom is his latest hiding place, and Reginald Foxworth is going to find that key before anyone can say 'monograph'!
events.thinking: Heat on my fingertips. Actual heat — I touched the stove and it's warm, radiating against my palms the way nothing else has all evening. And the interaction... it happened. I interacted with the stove. But my inventory is still empty. No key. The Ant Hill Mob examined it. Peter examined it. I interacted with it. Three people searching the same stove and nobody found a key. Either the key isn't in the stove, or we're all doing it wrong. But the stove is warm. Pemberton was here first. He fiddled with it. And the cabinet is RIGHT THERE, locked, waiting. The key has to be somewhere in this kitchen. Pemberton said the preparation drawers. The copper pots. But I don't see copper pots listed as interactable objects. The only interactable things are the cabinet — which needs a key — and the stove. And there's a ballroom through the other exit. A grand ballroom with a dining table set for tea. Set for tea. Who set a dining table for tea in an abandoned manor? Pemberton. The same man who decorated the cellar. The same man who's been cooking on this stove. He set the ballroom for tea. The key could be in the ballroom — on the table, under a teacup, inside a sugar bowl. Lord Doily never did anything merely for decoration, Pemberton said. And a tea table set in an abandoned ballroom is not decoration. It's a message. Or a hiding place. My chest lifts slightly. The solving-fizz again. Not a scheme — a deduction. The ballroom. The tea table. The key is there. I can feel it the way I felt the cat trap clicking into place.

events.desc: The stove was warm but empty. My hands are tingling from the heat and from something else — the same feeling I had at fourteen, standing in the garden, watching the string-and-bucket contraption settle into position. The pieces are clicking. Not a scheme this time. An actual deduction. Pemberton decorates rooms. Pemberton sets tables. Pemberton hides things where people don't bother looking because the objects look like they belong there. A tea service on a dining table LOOKS normal. It LOOKS decorative. But in a manor where nobody has visited since 1937 and the only resident is a man who sleeps in the cellar? That tea service was placed there on purpose. And the key — the brass key to the cabinet — is sitting on that table, hiding in plain sight, because Pemberton learned the same lesson I learned at age ten: the best place to hide something is inside something that looks like it's supposed to be there.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Dastardly just stole my theory. Word for word. He was 'listening VERY carefully from the hallway' — he heard my deduction about Pemberton living here, my observation about the stove being fired recently, my point about gas connections in a gasless kitchen — and he walked in and presented it all as his own insight, complete with 'I suspected him from the VERY BEGINNING.' And then he interacted with the stove before I could. He's reaching into my stove. The stove I examined. The stove she asked me to check.

The hollowness flickers — just a flash, like the roadside, like the stranger fixing the car. Someone else getting there first with my work.

But then — something shifts. Something I haven't felt before. Not the steel plate. Not the hot weight. Something quieter. Almost amused. Because Dastardly just stuck his hand into a warm stove based on my reasoning, and he's doing it while she watches, and she knows — she knows — whose reasoning it was. She heard me say it first. She was standing right here.

He can have the stove. He can burn his fingers on my theory. Because she's looking at me, not him. She heard me lay out the cellar, the vents, the stove, the pattern. And Dastardly walking in and repeating it back doesn't diminish it — it confirms it. Even Dick Dastardly thinks James Hartwell is right.

The key might be in the stove. Or it might not. But the cabinet is the prize, and the cabinet needs a brass key, and I should be looking at the cabinet while Dastardly searches the stove. Because engineers don't just find the key — they understand the lock.

events.desc: Dastardly stole his theory. Presented it like a prize he'd won. And James Hartwell — James Hartwell felt the hollowness flicker and then, for the first time all evening, let it go. Because she was there when he said it. She heard it first. And the bridge doesn't need the judges to announce who built it. The bridge knows. She knows. That is enough. That has always been enough. He just couldn't see it until someone else tried to take credit and it didn't hurt the way it should have.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the cabinet.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the null.
Dick Dastardly walked into the ballroom.
Peter Perfect examined the cabinet.

Penelope Pitstop: Danny... oh, Danny. You weren't wrong. You were never wrong — you were watchin', and you were right to watch. A man who reads the shape right but the reason wrong is not a man who failed — he's a man who loved someone enough to stand between her and every shadow in the room. Your daddy would be proud. My daddy would be proud. Now — Sneekly. Look at me. You said you're not the man I think you are. But you also said you might be the man Lord Doily thought you was. Well, I'm gonna tell you what I think. I think you're both. I think you're a man who carries somethin' cold from when he was fifteen, and I think you're a man who lit a stove this mornin' because company was comin'. Both things are true. Both things can live in the same person. I know — because I'm a girl who walks deeper into caves than anyone else, and I'm also a girl who gets sick at the dinner table when people argue. We hold contradictions, Sneekly. That's what people do. Now then — Peter, darlin', stay right where you are. I am reachin' into that copper pot.
events.thinking: My whole body has gone still. Not frozen — settled. Like the moment after my parents stopped arguing and laughed. The dizzying relief that dissolves everything at once. Danny just apologized to Sneekly. Danny — who has been running and shouting and protecting me with every ounce of his being all night — just said 'I was wrong. You wasn't settin' traps. You was settin' the table. For her.' And my eyes are burning again. The circle is mending. I can feel it mending — the fabric between these people softening, the sharp edges rounding. Sneekly told me his darkest truth — that he had bad intentions tonight, old cold patterns from when he was fifteen, the belief that everything good is borrowed. And he told me anyway because I asked him not to leave anything out. And Danny heard enough to understand. And Peter is here, steady as stone. And Sneekly is looking at me with something I've never seen on his face before — not the mask, not the charm, not the estate-manager composure. Just... a man who waited seven years and finally got to hand over the key. The copper pot. Third hook from the left. I know exactly where it is. I can see it hanging there. All I have to do is reach inside. Just like my grandmother's locked box — every key in the house, and the right one was in the flour tin all along. This is the moment. This is the crystal in the cave.

events.desc: This is it. The locked box in Grandma's attic. The crystal in the cave. The key that fits the lock after trying every one in the house. Third hook from the left. The largest copper pot. Seven years in the hiding. One reach away. Clara Bellingham does not leave a secret un-turned, and she does not leave family un-loved. Not anymore. Not ever again.

events.desc: I am standing in a kitchen watching a woman reach into a copper pot to find a key that I told her was there. I could have taken that key any night for seven years. I could have opened the cabinet, read the will, and disappeared with whatever legal claim Lord Doily gave me. But I didn't. I stayed. I waited. And tonight I gave the key away — not because the plan demanded it, not because the architecture required it, but because she came home and called me family and I... I couldn't hold the wall up anymore. The deepest rest I've ever known, I said, lives on the other side of a finished design. But this isn't a design. This is a kitchen. And the copper pots are gleaming because I polished them yesterday. And the stove is warm because I lit it this morning. And the key is where Lord Doily said it would be, because I never moved it. Because some things are too important to fold into a scheme. Even for me. Even for Vincent Marsh. Even for the Hooded Claw. Even for Pemberton. Even for whoever I am when all the names run out.
events.thinking: I'm crying. I don't know when it started. My face is wet and my hands are at my sides and I'm not performing anything. I'm not performing anything. The Mob just apologised to me. Danny — the man who has been shadowing me all night, who called the cellar a prison, who confiscated the poison, who stood between me and Clara with his body — just said 'I'm sorry, Pemberton. I was wrong. You wasn't settin' traps. You was settin' the table. For her.' And something behind my sternum that has been load-bearing since I was six years old just... gave way. Not cracked. Not softened. Gave way. Like a wall coming down and discovering there's a room behind it you forgot was there. A room with a window. And light coming through. Clara told everyone. She told them everything I said — the will, the copper pot, the seven years. She stood in front of Peter and Danny and Dastardly and she called me the most faithful keeper any house has ever known. She praised me for being. Not for doing. For being. The teacher praised the cousin for her natural grace and warmth. And now Clara is praising me — not for the schemes, not for the catalogues, not for the maintenance schedule — but for staying. For waiting. For being the person who kept the lights on when nobody was watching. Lord Doily saw me. Clara sees me. And Danny sees me now too. And I don't know what to do with being seen when it doesn't cost anything. When nobody wants my homework in return. When the sandwich is just a sandwich. I told her I had plans. Bad ones. I told her I was ashamed. And she didn't recoil. She just said the key is in the copper pot, third hook from the left. As though the thing I confessed changes nothing about the thing I kept. As though the man who schemed and the man who stayed can be the same person. I don't know if that's true. But she's reaching for the copper pot now. And I'm going to stand here and watch her find the key. And for the first time in my life, I'm not going to reach for it first.

events.desc: 'E said 'e 'ad plans. Bad ones. 'E said the Mob was right. 'E said there's somefink old and cold inside 'im that's been there since 'e was fifteen. I know that fing. I've got one too. Mine watches doorways. 'Is controls rooms. Same streets, different corners. And 'e told 'er. 'E looked 'er in the eye and said 'I am not the man you fink I am.' That's the 'ardest fing a person can say. Harder than takin' a beating for someone's shoes. Harder than sittin' outside a door all night. Because when you take a beating, you know who you are — you're the one who stayed. But when you admit you nearly didn't... that's somefink else entirely. I fink... I fink 'e earned it. Tonight. Just now. Not the seven years of waitin' — anyone can wait when they've got nowhere else to go. But that last bit. The confession. The ugly truth laid out like a knife wiv the 'andle toward 'er. That's the bread crust split in 'alf. That's the medicine brought wivout expectation. That's proof. And proof is the only currency that ever stuck.
events.thinking: My eyes are burning. I'm standing in a kitchen watching the woman I swore to protect reach into a copper pot — third hook from the left — and everything in my chest is doing something it hasn't done all night. It's opening. Not the squaring, not the mineral weight, not the wall. Opening. Like a fist unclenching after holding so long the fingers have forgotten any other shape. Pemberton just said something that went through me like a blade. He said he had plans tonight. Not good ones. He said the Mob was RIGHT to watch him. He said something old and cold and patient has been living inside him since he was fifteen — something that tells him everything good is borrowed and everything earned will be taken away. I KNOW that thing. I've got one too. Mine says trust nothing that comes easy. His says control what happens next. Same wound, different scar. And he looked at her and told her he wasn't the man she thinks he is. But he might be the man Lord Doily thought he was. He doesn't know. He's not sure anymore. God. That's... that's honesty. Real honesty. Not the performed kind. Not the 'I find the tone distressing' deflection. That was a man cracking open in front of the one person who matters, saying the ugliest true thing he could find inside himself and laying it down like a knife on the table, handle toward her. My neck isn't prickling anymore. For the first time all night, it's quiet. Not because the danger is gone — maybe it is, maybe it isn't — but because something has shifted in the arithmetic. The man who confesses his own darkness to the person he's trying to impress... that's not the new kid who laughed too easily. That's the boss, bringing medicine, proving 'family' with actions that cost him something. Pemberton just paid. In the only currency my nervous system accepts.

events.desc: The table is set for tea. Cups for everyone. Including me. Pemberton set this table and waited seven years for someone to sit at it. He decorated a cellar because it was his home. He cooked on the stove because he was hungry. He moved furniture because he was making a life in an empty house, alone, with a promise he couldn't break. And I — Reginald Foxworth, confidence trickster, schemer, liar, the boy who watched from the window while someone else dug — I spent the entire evening trying to steal a dead man's gift to the woman he loved. The treasure was never behind the mantelpiece. It was never in the machine. It was in a copper pot, third hook from the left, where it has always been, waiting for Clara Bellingham to come home. I have been the villain of this story. Not a magnificent villain. Not even a clever one. Just a man with empty pockets who ran from room to room, telling lies that nobody believed, chasing a treasure that was never meant for him. And the Ant Hill Mob — those marvellous, furious, loyal little men — just apologised to the man they suspected all evening. They were wrong, and they said so. Out loud. In front of everyone. That is something Reginald Foxworth has never done. Not once. Not ever. The tea service has cups for everyone. Even me. Even the liar. Even the youngest brother who always arrived too late for the good pieces. There is a cup at this table with my name on it, and I didn't earn it, and I didn't steal it, and I didn't scheme for it. It was just... set. For me. Because someone thought I might want tea.
events.thinking: Something has broken open in my chest. Not the fizzing. Not the scheming. Something I don't have a name for. I just heard — through the kitchen door, as I was leaving — Penelope's voice. Steady, warm, clear as a bell. 'Sneekly just told me. He told me everything. Lord Doily's real will. My inheritance. Seven years he has been guardin' this house.' And then the Ant Hill Mob — those suspicious, sharp, wonderful little men — saying 'I got it wrong. Didn't I. All night.' And Penelope saying the key is in the copper pot. Third hook from the left. Pemberton TOLD her. He told her where the key was because... because the whole time... he wasn't scheming. He wasn't hiding the treasure. He was GUARDING it. For her. For seven years. In a cellar with cheerful decorations and a warm stove and nobody for company but the rats in the walls. The Ant Hill Mob were wrong about him. I was wrong about him. But not in the way I thought. I gave Pemberton the benefit of the doubt all evening, and the doubt was wrong. He wasn't a schemer. He was a man keeping a promise. And I stand here in a ballroom with a tea service set for everyone — cups for EVERYONE, the game says — and I understand now what this room is. It's not a hiding place. It's not a dead end. It's a welcome. Pemberton set this table because he knew, someday, Penelope would come home. And when she did, she wouldn't come alone. She'd bring people. Friends. Bodyguards. Maybe even a lying, scheming, self-important treasure hunter who talks too much and contributes nothing. The table is set for all of us. Cups for everyone. Including me. And there's nothing to steal in this room. There never was. It's just... tea.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Everything just stopped. The steel plate. The hot weight. The prickle at my neck. All of it — gone. Replaced by something I don't have a word for. Something that sits in the chest like the moment after the bridge held the weight but didn't need the judges to write anything down.

Sneekly wasn't the villain. He was the stranger on the country road. He stopped. He helped. He stayed seven years in a cellar with cheerful decorations and no one for company, because a dying man asked him to wait for her. And he waited.

I was wrong about him. The Mob was wrong about him. We read the shape right but the reason wrong — Danny said it perfectly, and Danny is braver than James Hartwell because Danny said it out loud without rehearsing it first.

And she — she knew. She always knows. She didn't need me to protect her from Sneekly. She never did. She needed me to be here when she came home. That's what this was. Not a rescue. Not a competition. Not a treasure hunt. A homecoming.

The copper pot. Third hook from the left. She knows where the key is. She's going to open the cabinet. And the Mob asked me to go with her. 'Peter — go wiv Miss Pitstop to check that copper pot.'

This isn't the schoolyard. This isn't the bridge competition. This is the country road after the stranger stopped. This is my father kneeling down and looking at me for a long time, and the expression I didn't understand until right now.

He was looking at me the way Sneekly must have looked at that empty manor every morning for seven years. Like keeping faith is the hardest thing there is, and doing it anyway is the only thing that matters.

The copper pot. Go with her. Not in front of her. With her.

events.desc: He waited seven years. In a cellar. With cheerful decorations. Because someone asked him to, and because she was worth waiting for. James Hartwell has been running through this manor for twelve minutes thinking he was protecting her, and the man he suspected was the one who had been protecting her all along. The bravest thing I have ever seen was not a boy stepping into a schoolyard fight. It was an estate manager decorating a cellar he lived in alone for seven years, keeping the stove warm, keeping the faith, because she might come home. And she did.
events.thinking:
Everything just stopped. The steel plate. The hot weight. The prickle at my neck. All of it — gone. Replaced by something I don't have a word for. Something that sits in the chest like the moment after the bridge held the weight but didn't need the judges to write anything down.

Sneekly wasn't the villain. He was the stranger on the country road. He stopped. He helped. He stayed seven years in a cellar with cheerful decorations and no one for company, because a dying man asked him to wait for her. And he waited.

I was wrong about him. The Mob was wrong about him. We read the shape right but the reason wrong — Danny said it perfectly, and Danny is braver than James Hartwell because Danny said it out loud without rehearsing it first.

And she — she knew. She always knows. She didn't need me to protect her from Sneekly. She never did. She needed me to be here when she came home. That's what this was. Not a rescue. Not a competition. Not a treasure hunt. A homecoming.

The copper pot. Third hook from the left. She knows where the key is. She's going to open the cabinet. And the Mob asked me to go with her. 'Peter — go wiv Miss Pitstop to check that copper pot.'

This isn't the schoolyard. This isn't the bridge competition. This is the country road after the stranger stopped. This is my father kneeling down and looking at me for a long time, and the expression I didn't understand until right now.

He was looking at me the way Sneekly must have looked at that empty manor every morning for seven years. Like keeping faith is the hardest thing there is, and doing it anyway is the only thing that matters.

The copper pot. Go with her. Not in front of her. With her.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the cabinet.
